$$ \displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}\sum_{a=1}^{j}\sum_{b=j+1}^{n}\frac{\langle{j,j+1}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha j}\rangle\langle{\alpha,j+1}\rangle}\langle{\alpha a}\rangle[ab]\langle{b\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle=\sum_{1\leq a<b\leq n}\langle{\alpha a}\rangle[ab]\langle{b\alpha}\rangle\sum_{j=a}^{b-1}\frac{\langle{j,j+1}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha j}\rangle\langle{\alpha,j+1}\rangle} \displaystyle=\sum_{1\leq a<b\leq n}\langle{\alpha a}\rangle[ab]\langle{b\alpha}\rangle\frac{\langle{ab}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha a}\rangle\langle{\alpha b}\rangle} \displaystyle=-\sum_{1\leq a<b\leq n}[ab]\langle{ab}\rangle \displaystyle=-(p_{1}+\ldots+p_{n})^{2} $$

using $2p_{a}\!\cdot p_{b}=\langle{ab}\rangle[ab]$ , and this concludes the proof. Note that in the second line we used a telescoped version of the the Schouten identity (i.e. the ‘eikonal’ identity) which is

$$ \frac{\langle{12}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle}+\frac{\langle{23}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle\langle{\alpha 3}\rangle}=\frac{\langle{13}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{\alpha 3}\rangle}. $$

#### SDYM current examples

Let us give some low-point examples for all-plus partial currents. The two-point partial current is given by a single three-point diagram, and is

$$ J_{\rm YM}(1,2)=\frac{\sqrt{2}g\langle{\alpha|12|\alpha}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{2}}\frac{i}{(p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}}=-i\sqrt{2}g\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle}\frac{1}{\langle{12}\rangle}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle}. $$

The three-point partial current is given by two diagrams, drawn in figure 11.

*Figure 11: The two color ordered Feynman diagrams contributing to $J_{\rm YM}(1,2,3)$ .*

The expression from the Feynman diagrams is

$$ J_{\rm YM}(1,2,3)=\frac{(i\sqrt{2}g)^{2}}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha 3}\rangle^{2}}\left(\frac{\langle{\alpha|12|\alpha}\rangle}{(p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(1+2)3|\alpha}\rangle}{(p_{1}+p_{2}+p_{3})^{2}}+\frac{\langle{\alpha|23|\alpha}\rangle}{(p_{2}+p_{3})^{2}}\frac{\langle{\alpha|1(2+3)|\alpha}\rangle}{(p_{1}+p_{2}+p_{3})^{2}}\right), $$

and can be shown to be identically equal to the resummed Parke-Taylor-like formula

$$ J_{\rm YM}(1,2,3)=(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{2}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle}\frac{1}{\langle{12}\rangle\langle{23}\rangle}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 3}\rangle}. $$

This equality of course holds without the use of momentum conservation.

### Why are we calling them “currents”?

Let us briefly explain why we call these objects “currents.” In this note we work with the lightcone scalars. However, if one uses the usual vector field $A_{\mu}$ , the all-plus current would have a free space-time index and would be equal to our expression times a factor $\langle{\alpha|\sigma_{\mu}(p_{1}+\ldots+p_{n})|\alpha}\rangle$ . This factor vanishes when contracted with $(p_{1}+\ldots+p_{n})^{\mu}$ , which is related to gauge invariance. After Fourier-transforming the off-shell leg, this is the equation of a conserved current, hence the name “current.”

### 8.2 Gravity all-plus current

Now we turn to gravity. We write down the gravity all-plus current recursion relation displayed in figure 10. It is

$$ p_{N}^{2}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(N)=-\frac{\kappa}{2}\sum_{A,B|A\cup B=N}\langle\alpha|p_{A}p_{B}|\alpha\rangle^{2}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(A)\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(B). $$

In gravity there is no notion of color ordering and we sum over all subsets $A$ and $B$ such that $A\cup B=N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ , neither $A$ nor $B$ is empty and $A\cap B=\emptyset$ . In this sum $A$ and $B$ are indistinguishable, so if the pair $(A,B)$ is included in the sum then we do not independently include $(B,A)$ .

The base case of the all-plus current is just the polarization factor

$$ \mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(i)=\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{4}}. $$

The recursion relation is solved by the “tree formula”

$$ \displaystyle\boxed{\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1,\ldots,n)=\left(-\frac{\kappa}{2}\right)^{n-1}\left(\prod_{a=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha a}\rangle^{4}}\right)\sum_{\text{trees}}\sum_{\text{edges }(ij)}\frac{[ij]}{\langle ij\rangle}\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha j}\rangle^{2}.} $$

In this formula, the “trees” in question are not the cubic Feynman trees but rather a different kind of tree. They are trees where each node corresponds to a positive-helicity graviton $1\ldots n$ and every node is allowed to have arbitrarily many connections. An example is drawn in figure 12.

*Figure 12: Example of a tree that contributes to $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1,\ldots,8)$ , along with the factor of a single edge.*

Each edge comes with a factor of $\frac{[ij]}{\langle{ij}\rangle}\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha j}\rangle^{2}$ . The tree-formula can also be expressed as

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1,\ldots,n) \displaystyle=\left(-\frac{\kappa}{2}\right)^{n-1}\sum_{\text{trees}}\sum_{\text{edges }(ij)}\frac{[ij]}{\langle ij\rangle}\prod_{a=1}^{n}\langle\alpha a\rangle^{2(\mathrm{deg}(a)-2)} $$

where $\mathrm{deg}(a)$ denotes the number of neighbors the node has, or its “degree.” The degrees of the nodes in a tree diagram satisfy the relation

$$ \sum_{a=1}^{n}(\text{deg}(a)-2)=-2. $$

There is another expression for the all-plus current which we’ll write down. Utilizing the matrix tree theorem [95], if one defines the matrix

$$ \Psi_{ij}=\begin{cases}-\frac{[ij]}{\langle{ij}\rangle}\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha j}\rangle^{2}&\text{if }i\neq j\\
\sum_{k=1,k\neq i}^{n}\frac{[ik]}{\langle{ik}\rangle}\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha k}\rangle^{2}&\text{if }i=j\end{cases} $$

then $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}$ can be expressed via

$$ \mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1,\ldots,n)=\left(-\frac{\kappa}{2}\right)^{n-1}\left(\prod_{a=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha a}\rangle^{4}}\right)|\Psi|^{i}_{i}. $$

Here, $|\Psi|^{i}_{i}$ is the determinant of the minor of the matrix $\Psi$ where the $i^{\rm th}$ row and column have been removed. It can be shown that the expression is independent what choice of $i=1,\ldots,n$ one makes.

We write down the proof of the tree formula in appendix D.

### SDG current examples

The two-point current is given by a single cubic Feynman diagram. It is

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1,2)=\frac{i\kappa}{2}\frac{\langle{\alpha|12|\alpha}\rangle^{2}}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{4}\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{4}}\frac{i}{(p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}}. $$

The expression can be simplified to

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1,2) \displaystyle=-\frac{\kappa}{2}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{2}}\frac{[12]}{\langle{12}\rangle}. $$

This expression for $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1,2)$ corresponds to the single tree in figure 13.

*Figure 13: The one tree which contributes to $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1,2).$*

Now let’s look at the three-point example. Here there are three contributing Feynman diagrams, shown in figure 14.

*Figure 14: Three Feynman diagrams contributing to $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1,2,3)$ .*

Summing the three Feynman diagrams, we get

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1,2,3)=\left(-\frac{\kappa}{2}\right)^{2} \displaystyle\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{4}\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{4}\langle{\alpha 3}\rangle^{4}}\Bigg(\frac{\langle{\alpha|12|\alpha}\rangle^{2}}{(p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(1+2)3|\alpha}\rangle^{2}}{(p_{1}+p_{2}+p_{3})^{2}} \displaystyle+\frac{\langle{\alpha|23|\alpha}\rangle^{2}}{(p_{2}+p_{3})^{2}}\frac{\langle{\alpha|1(2+3)|\alpha}\rangle^{2}}{(p_{1}+p_{2}+p_{3})^{2}}+\frac{\langle{\alpha|13|\alpha}\rangle^{2}}{(p_{1}+p_{3})^{2}}\frac{\langle{\alpha|2(1+3)|\alpha}\rangle^{2}}{(p_{1}+p_{2}+p_{3})^{2}}\Bigg). $$

This expression is identically equal to

$$ \mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1,2,3)=\left(-\frac{\kappa}{2}\right)^{2}\left(\frac{[12]}{\langle{12}\rangle}\frac{[23]}{\langle{23}\rangle}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha 3}\rangle^{2}}+\frac{[13]}{\langle{13}\rangle}\frac{[32]}{\langle{32}\rangle}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha 3}\rangle^{2}}+\frac{[21]}{\langle{21}\rangle}\frac{[13]}{\langle{13}\rangle}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha 3}\rangle^{2}}\right) $$

which corresponds to the three trees drawn in figure 15. Note that this equality does not require momentum conservation.

*Figure 15: Three trees contributing to $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1,2,3)$ .*

We emphasize that the tree sum is different from the Feynman diagram sum. It is not the case that each tree corresponds to a Feynman diagram. Rather, it is the sum of trees that is equal to the sum of Feynman diagrams. The trees should be thought of as the gravitational analog of color orderings in Yang-Mills theory.

### History of the tree formula

The history of the tree formula (134) is a bit complicated. If one likes, one could in retrospect attribute it to Bern, Dixon, Perelstein, Rozowsky [50]. While they did not write this formula exactly, they did give formulae for it which are ultimately equivalent, including one using Young tableaux. They were aware of the trees, or “elk diagrams,” at least when it came to the structure of square brackets in the numerators. Importantly, the authors also knew that their expression for the all-plus current was (essentially) equal to an expression for gravity MHV amplitudes, which they checked by comparing it to the old-fashioned KLT inspired Berends-Giele-Kuijf formula [96]. The trees were later independently discovered by Nguyen, Spradlin, Volovich, and Wen [97] who gave closed-form expression for MHV amplitudes as a sum over trees. Using these two papers, the tree formula for the all-plus current could then be deduced. The situation was spelled out clearly in a paper by Krasnov, Scarinci [98] and then also Delfino [94], who showed how the tree-formula itself follows from the all-plus Berends-Giele recursion relation. See also [61] where it is shown how to calculate the MHV amplitudes using the all-plus current in the perturbiner framework. Various tree formulae also appear throughout the study of twistor (string) theory in many different contexts. See [99, 100, 101, 102, 103] and section 6 of [104].

### 8.3 Vanishing of the tree-level-one-minus amplitudes

Now that we have computed the all-plus off-shell currents, we are in a position to see why the tree-level-one-minus amplitudes vanish (except at 3-pts).

One can extract the tree-level-one-minus amplitudes from the all-plus currents by requiring that the off-shell leg $p_{m}=-(p_{1}+\ldots+p_{n})$ be on-shell, before amputating the $p_{m}^{2}$ propagator and multiplying the expression by the minus-particle’s polarization factor.

So, in gauge theory

$$ \mathcal{A}^{\rm tree}(1^{a_{1}+},\ldots,n^{a_{n}+},m^{a_{m}-})=i\langle{\alpha m}\rangle^{2}(p_{1}+\ldots+p_{n})^{2}\mathcal{J}_{\rm YM}(1^{a_{1}},\ldots,n^{a_{n}})^{a_{m}} $$

and in gravity

$$ \mathcal{M}^{\rm tree}(1^{+},\ldots,n^{+},m^{-})=i\langle{\alpha m}\rangle^{4}(p_{1}+\ldots+p_{n})^{2}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1,\ldots,n). $$

However, because, $(p_{1}+\ldots+p_{n})^{2}=p_{m}^{2}=0$ , this implies the tree-level-one-minus amplitudes vanish!

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{\rm tree}(1^{a_{1}+},\ldots,n^{a_{n}+},m^{a_{m}-})=0\,,\hskip 14.22636pt\mathcal{M}^{\rm tree}(1^{+},\ldots,n^{+},m^{-})=0\,,\hskip 14.22636pt\text{ for }n>2. $$

The reason this happens is that the all-plus currents (125) and (134) have only holomorphic collinear singularities, i.e. singularities of the form $\frac{1}{\langle{ij}\rangle}$ as $\langle{ij}\rangle\to 0$ . In a typical theory, like the scalar $\varphi^{3}$ theory, tree-level amplitudes have multiparticle singularities when internal propagators $\frac{1}{P^{2}}$ go on shell. However, in SDYM and SDG, the multiparticle $\frac{1}{P^{2}}$ singularities that appear in each Feynman diagram are actually spurious, and after all the diagrams are added together the only remaining singularities are the two-particle holomorphic collinear ones. Because there is, in particular, no term in the currents like $\frac{1}{(p_{1}+\ldots+p_{n})^{2}}$ , the factor of $(p_{1}+\ldots+p_{n})^{2}$ that comes from amputating the final leg does not cancel with anything in the denominator, which is why the overall expression becomes zero as $p_{m}^{2}\to 0$ . However, this argument does not render the 3-pt amplitudes zero. For instance, if we use $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1,2)$ from (140), we have

$$ \mathcal{M}^{\rm tree}(1^{+},2^{+},3^{-})=i\langle{\alpha 3}\rangle^{4}(\langle{12}\rangle[12])\left(-\frac{\kappa}{2}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{2}}\frac{[12]}{\langle{12}\rangle}\right) $$

which doesn’t vanish due to the special nature of 3-pt kinematics.

(As an aside, another simple way to see the tree-level-one-minus amplitudes generically vanish follows from making the special choice of reference spinor $|\alpha\rangle\to|m\rangle$ .)

There is however a loophole to our discussion. What if all holomorphic inner products are zero, i.e. what if $\langle{ij}\rangle=0$ for all $i$ , $j$ ? Then the currents would be singular, not zero. In a set of recent works [1, 2, 3] this idea was explored and non-zero, distributional, expressions for the tree-level-one-minus amplitudes were found in the “half collinear” regime where all angle brackets $|i\rangle$ are proportional to each other. Note that this kinematic configuration is not possible for physical particles in $(1,3)$ signature. Actually, the non-vanishing of the three-point $+$ $+$ $-$ amplitudes can be seen as a special case of this story. This is because momentum conservation among three massless particles requires that either $|1\rangle\propto|2\rangle\propto|3\rangle$ or $|1]\propto|2]\propto|3]$ .

### 8.4 Another recursive formula for the all-plus currents from collinear limits

The all-plus currents for gauge theory and gravity satisfy another pair of recursive formulae aside from the Berends-Giele one. These recursion relations come from the fact that the currents only have holomorphic collinear singularities, and should ultimately be understood as arising from the integrability of the classical theory.

For SDYM, this recursion relation is

$$ \boxed{\mathcal{J}_{\rm YM}(1^{a_{1}},\ldots,n^{a_{n}})^{a_{m}}=\sqrt{2}g\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{f^{a_{n}a_{i}c}}{\langle{ni}\rangle}\frac{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}\mathcal{J}_{\rm YM}(1^{a_{1}},\ldots,i^{c},\ldots,(n\!-\!1)^{a_{n-1}})^{a_{m}}.} $$

Note that all of the holomorphic collinear singularities of the LHS where $\langle{ni}\rangle\to 0$ for some $i$ can be read off from this formula.

At the level of the color-ordered partial currents using $[T^{a},T^{b}]=if^{abc}T^{c}$ , if particle $n$ is inserted in between, say, some particles $i$ and $j$ in the color ordering, the above recursion relation is equivalent to

$$ J_{\rm YM}(\ldots,i,n,j,\ldots)=i\sqrt{2}g\left(\frac{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}\frac{1}{\langle{ni}\rangle}-\frac{\langle{\alpha j}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}\frac{1}{\langle{nj}\rangle}\right)J_{\rm YM}(\ldots,i,j,\ldots). $$

The above formula can easily be checked to be true straight from the Schouten identity

$$ \left(\frac{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}\frac{1}{\langle{ni}\rangle}-\frac{\langle{\alpha j}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}\frac{1}{\langle{nj}\rangle}\right)=-\frac{\langle{ij}\rangle}{\langle{in}\rangle\langle{nj}\rangle} $$

when applied to the Parke-Taylor-like expression for $J_{\rm YM}$ (125). In the special case that the particle $n$ finds itself on the edge of the color ordering, the recursion relation reads

$$ J_{\rm YM}(1,\ldots,n\!-\!1,n)=-i\sqrt{2}g\frac{\langle{\alpha,n\!-\!1}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}\frac{1}{\langle{n\!-\!1,n}\rangle}J_{\rm YM}(1,\ldots,n\!-\!1) $$

which is even more easily checked to be true from (125).

The reason that (147) holds is the meromorphicity of the all-plus current expression (125). In particular, both the left and right sides of the equation have all the “correct” holomorphic collinear poles $\langle{ni}\rangle\to 0$ . Importantly, this uses the fact that $|n\rangle$ is an unconstrained variable in $\mathbb{C}P^{1}$ . In this context, the “correct” pole is the one given by the 3-pt Feynman vertex, as we’ll discuss more in section 9.3. Equation (147) is then simply a sum over all of the expected residues as $|n\rangle$ approaches each of the points $|i\rangle$ .

In gravity, the analogous recursive formula is

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(|1\rangle,|1],\ldots,|n\rangle,|n]) \displaystyle=-\frac{\kappa}{2}\,\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}}{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle^{2}}\frac{[ni]}{\langle{ni}\rangle}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(|1\rangle,|1],\ldots,|i\rangle,|i]+\frac{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle}|n],\ldots,|n\!-\!1\rangle,|n\!-\!1]).\;\;\;\vphantom{\Bigg\rvert} $$

Notice that this equation modifies the square bracket of particle $i$ on the RHS. The SDYM current does not depend on the square brackets, so the recursive formula (147) did not display this feature.

This formula was guessed by BDPR in [51], see their (6.5), and then effectively proven to be true in their appendix C.1. It was however written down more clearly in the above form and proven by Krasnov and Scarinci in [98, 94] using natural tree/matrix identities, where it was related to Hodges’ BCFW inverse-soft recursion relation [105, 106, 107, 108] for MHV amplitudes via the NSVW formula. It was then accidentally rediscovered by the author in the context of $\text{L}\mathfrakalt{w}_{1+\infty}$ symmetry in [109]. We discuss this relation more in section 14.

*Figure 16: Left: If $|n\rangle\to|i\rangle$ , the only singular trees in $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}$ are ones where the nodes $n$ and $i$ are adjacent. Right: In this limit, we can consider $i$ and $n$ as belonging to a single node with parameters $|i\rangle$ , $|i]+|n]$ , multiplied by an extra factor to account for the edge between $i$ and $n$ .*

We’ve put the proof of this formula in appendix E. Here, we’ll simply explain why this formula exhibits the correct holomorphic collinear limits as $|n\rangle\to|i\rangle$ .

The key idea is drawn in figure 16. If $|n\rangle\to|i\rangle$ , then the only singular terms come from trees where the nodes $i$ and $n$ are adjacent. All the other neighboring nodes in the tree then have the option of connecting to either $i$ or $n$ . We can therefore think of the $i$ - $n$ edge as a single node itself, with an angle bracket of $|i\rangle$ and a square bracket of $|i]+|n]$ . (If one foils out the connection between a neighboring node and the square bracket $|i]+|n]$ , one reproduces the sum over trees whose edges could have connected to either $i$ or $n$ .) Therefore, in the holomorphic collinear limit the tree formula (134) reproduces that of the RHS of (151), which is

$$ \lim_{|n\rangle\to|i\rangle}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1,2,3,\ldots,n)=-\frac{\kappa}{2}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle^{4}}\frac{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle^{2}[ni]\langle{i\alpha}\rangle^{2}}{\langle{ni}\rangle}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(\ldots,|i\rangle,|i]+|n],\ldots). $$

This is also the correct holomorphic collinear limit one can calculate directly from the 3-pt vertex.

## 9 Basic properties of the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes

Let us now start our discussion of the one-loop-all-plus-amplitudes of SDYM and SDG by reviewing their basic properties.

### 9.1 Rationality

The cutting rules state that the analytic discontinuity of a one-loop amplitude with respect to a particular kinematic invariant occurs when the momenta passing through the appropriate cut of the loop go on shell [110]. So if one “cuts” the amplitude through the loop and demands that the two tree-level sub-amplitudes independently obey momentum conservation, and then sums over all possible internal particles that can run through the cut, one can compute the discontinuity.

For the case of the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes in pure YM and pure gravity, the possibilities are drawn in figure 17. The discontinuity is either given by two on-shell tree-level-one-minus amplitudes, or a tree-level MHV amplitude and a tree-level-all-plus amplitude. In both cases the cuts vanish and we can plainly see that there are no analytic discontinuities.

*Figure 17: The possible “cuts” of a one-loop-all-plus amplitude. Either both sides are one-minus amplitudes, which vanish, or one side is MHV and the other is all-plus, which also vanishes.*

If the amplitude has no branch cuts then its structure must be dramatically simpler than that of a generic one-loop amplitude. It cannot contain, say, polylogs or other special functions. It must be rational, i.e. be a ratio of angle and square brackets.

The one-loop-one-minus amplitudes must also be rational for the same reason.

### 9.2 Finiteness

Because the tree-level-all-plus amplitudes are zero, the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes are both IR and UV finite.

*Figure 18: One-loop IR divergences in gauge theory/gravity come from internal particles connecting external legs.*

IR divergences in YM/gravity one-loop amplitudes come from gluons/gravitons connecting two external legs. See figure 18. In the case of gauge theory, the IR divergence is proportional to [50]

$$ \text{IR div.}\sim\mathcal{A}_{n}^{\rm tree}\sum_{i\neq j}\left[-\frac{1}{\epsilon^{2}}+\frac{\ln(-s_{ij})}{\epsilon}\right] $$

where $\epsilon$ is the parameter in dimensional regularization, and in gravity the IR divergence is proportional to

$$ \text{IR div.}\sim\mathcal{M}_{n}^{\rm tree}\sum_{i\neq j}\left[s_{ij}\frac{\ln(-s_{ij})}{\epsilon}\right]. $$

For one-loop-all-plus amplitudes the IR divergence is therefore zero because the tree-level-all-plus amplitudes are zero.

Similarly, the UV divergence of the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes also vanishes because the tree-level-all-plus amplitudes are zero. Let us recall why. Think about pure Yang-Mills theory in any covariant gauge. The tree-level-all-plus amplitudes vanish because the numerators of these Feynman diagrams always contain a contraction between two positive-helicity polarization vectors, and one can always choose a residual gauge in which these vanish with $\varepsilon^{+}_{i}\cdot\varepsilon^{+}_{i^{\prime}}=0$ . Now, in the action, there is of course a propagator, a 3-pt vertex, and a 4-pt vertex which all get accompanying counterterms with the same kinematic structure. Because YM is renormalizable there are no more counterterms. So, if one wants to compute a one-loop-all-plus amplitude, the contributions from the tree diagrams containing a counterterm also vanish, once again due to the contractions between the polarization vectors. Therefore, because the counterterms will not enter the computation, the original amplitude must have been finite, and the coupling is automatically the renormalized one which matches tree-level amplitudes. The story works the same for gravity as the Einstein-Hilbert action is famously renormalizable at one loop [111] because the only possible counterterms that could be generated are either topological or are able to be removed by a field redefinition. At two-loops there is the Goroff-Sagnotti counterterm [112].

### 9.3 Holomorphic collinear limits

Consider a tree-level YM or gravity scattering amplitude which contains two positive-helicity gluons/gravitons with momenta $p_{1}$ and $p_{2}$ and

$$ p_{1}=|1\rangle[1|,\hskip 28.45274ptp_{2}=|2\rangle[2|. $$

Now imagine we take the holomorphic collinear limit

$$ |1\rangle\to|2\rangle. $$

If the two particles attach at a 3-pt vertex to an internal propagator with momentum $P$ , where

$$ P=p_{1}+p_{2} $$

then in this limit

$$ \displaystyle P\to|2\rangle \displaystyle([1|+[2|), \displaystyle P^{2} \displaystyle\to 0, $$

so $P$ goes on-shell and these diagrams develop a pole from the propagator. See figure 19.

*Figure 19: Tree-level amplitudes factorize as $P=p_{1}+p_{2}$ goes on shell.*

Therefore, in this limit, the only relevant diagrams are those where particles $1^{+}$ and $2^{+}$ connect at a 3-pt vertex before attaching to the rest of the diagram.

For gauge theory and gravity amplitudes, we express this as

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{|1\rangle\to|2\rangle}\mathcal{A}^{\rm tree}(1^{a+},2^{b+},\ldots) \displaystyle=\text{Split}^{1^{a+}2^{b+}}_{{\rm YM},P^{c-}}\,\mathcal{A}^{\rm tree}(P^{c+},\ldots)\,, \displaystyle\lim_{|1\rangle\to|2\rangle}\mathcal{M}^{\rm tree}(1^{+},2^{+},\ldots) \displaystyle=\text{Split}^{1^{+}2^{+}}_{{\rm G},P^{-}}\,\mathcal{M}^{\rm tree}(P^{+},\ldots)\,. $$

The formulae imply the tree-level amplitudes “factorize”. Note that the helicity of the $P$ particle in the splitting function $\text{Split}^{1^{+}2^{+}}_{P^{-}}$ is negative while in the amplitude it is positive, because the propagator is of the form $(+-)$ . That is, an incoming negative-helicity particle is the same as an outgoing positive-helicity particle.

*Figure 20: The diagram contributing to the $+$ $+$ $-$ splitting function.*

We can easily compute the on-shell 3-pt splitting function using the lightcone Feynman rules from section 7. See figure 20. Accounting for the appropriate polarization factors, vertex, and $P$ propagator, they are simply

$$ \displaystyle\text{Split}^{1^{a+}2^{b+}}_{{\rm YM},P^{c-}} \displaystyle=\frac{\langle{\alpha P}\rangle^{2}}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{2}}\times i\sqrt{2}gf^{abc}\langle{\alpha|12|\alpha}\rangle\times\frac{i}{\langle{12}\rangle[12]} \displaystyle=\sqrt{2}gf^{abc}\frac{1}{\langle{12}\rangle}\frac{\langle{\alpha P}\rangle^{2}}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle} $$

for Yang-Mills and

$$ \displaystyle\text{Split}^{1^{+}2^{+}}_{{\rm G},P^{-}} \displaystyle=\frac{\langle{\alpha P}\rangle^{4}}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{4}\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{4}}\times\frac{i\kappa}{2}\langle{\alpha|12|\alpha}\rangle^{2}\times\frac{i}{\langle{12}\rangle[12]} \displaystyle=-\frac{\kappa}{2}\frac{[12]}{\langle{12}\rangle}\frac{\langle{\alpha P}\rangle^{4}}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{2}} $$

for gravity. Similarly, one can also compute the $+$ $-$ $+$ splitting functions in the exact same way, and they are

$$ \text{Split}^{1^{a+}2^{b-}}_{{\rm YM},P^{c+}}=\sqrt{2}gf^{abc}\frac{1}{\langle{12}\rangle}\frac{\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{3}}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{\alpha P}\rangle^{2}},\hskip 21.33955pt\text{Split}^{1^{+}2^{-}}_{{\rm G},P^{+}}=-\frac{\kappa}{2}\frac{[12]}{\langle{12}\rangle}\frac{\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{6}}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha P}\rangle^{2}}. $$

Also, because there is no $+$ $+$ $+$ vertex, the associated splitting function is zero for gauge theory and gravity:

$$ \text{Split}^{1^{a+}2^{b+}}_{{\rm YM},P^{c+}}=0,\hskip 28.45274pt\text{Split}^{1^{+}2^{+}}_{{\rm G},P^{+}}=0. $$

Relevantly for us, the tree-level splitting functions are actually uncorrected in the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes! We can see why by looking at the structure of the self-dual lightcone diagrammatics. At one-loop level, there are two types of diagrams that become singular as $P$ goes on shell, drawn in figure 21.

*Figure 21: Two types of singular diagrams for one-loop-all-plus amplitudes as $P=p_{1}+p_{2}$ goes on-shell. The second type of diagram vanishes because tree-level-one-minus amplitudes are zero.*

In the first diagram, particles 1 and 2 connect at tree-level and the propagator connects to a lower-point one-loop-all-plus amplitude with $P$ on-shell. In the second diagram, we see a potential loop correction to the 3-pt splitting function, but the $P$ propagator connects to a tree-level-one-minus amplitude which vanishes as $P^{2}\to 0$ . So only the first type of diagram contributes, and the splitting function for one-loop-all-plus amplitudes equals the tree-level splitting function [113].

Actually, even though the above conclusion is correct, our reasoning was a bit hasty. There is also another type of contribution we need to consider, the “non-factorizing” contribution when particles 1 and 2 both connect directly to the loop itself. One might naively think that these diagrams won’t correct the splitting function because for generic values of the loop momentum $\ell$ there is no pole as $p_{1}\cdot p_{2}\to 0$ in the integrand. Nonetheless there do exist regimes of the loop momentum where a singularity could develop because an extra internal propagator could go on shell.

Consider for instance the configuration drawn in figure 22, which is the potentially problematic portion of a diagram, where we integrate over $\int d^{4}\ell$ . Consider the integral in the $\ell\approx 0$ region (where we continue the loop momentum in the integral to have euclidean signature). In the diagram we have the four propagators $1/\ell_{1}^{2}$ , $1/\ell_{2}^{2}$ , $1/\ell_{3}^{2}$ , $1/\ell_{n}^{2}$ , and if our theory is SDYM we have the three numerators $\langle{\alpha|1\ell|\alpha}\rangle$ , $\langle{\alpha|2(\ell+1)|\alpha}\rangle$ , $\langle{\alpha|n\ell|\alpha}\rangle$ .

*Figure 22: As $p_{1}\cdot p_{2}\to 0$ , diagrams of this type could develop a pole in $p_{1}\cdot p_{2}$ , but don’t for the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes after integration.*

For small $\ell$ , the four respective propagators are approximately $1/\ell_{1}^{2}=1/\ell^{2}$ , $1/\ell_{2}^{2}=1/(2\ell\cdot p_{1})$ , $1/\ell_{3}^{2}=1/(2\ell\cdot(p_{1}+p_{2})+2p_{1}\cdot p_{2})$ , and $1/\ell_{n}^{2}=1/(-2\ell\cdot p_{n})$ . Notice that the $1/\ell_{3}^{2}$ propagator goes on shell if $p_{1}\cdot p_{2}\to 0$ , but let’s see if this becomes a divergence after integration. Counting powers of $\ell$ from the numerator and denominator, we essentially have $\int d^{4}\ell\frac{\ell^{2}}{\ell^{5}}$ which vanishes over the $\ell\approx 0$ region due to the phase space factor. For SDG the integrand vanishes in this region even quicker, as the numerator is squared. So in conclusion, the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes do indeed enjoy the tree-level splitting relations

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{|1\rangle\to|2\rangle}\mathcal{A}^{\text{1-loop}}(1^{a+},2^{b+},\ldots,n^{a_{n}+}) \displaystyle=\text{Split}^{1^{a+}2^{b+}}_{{\rm YM},P^{c-}}\mathcal{A}^{\text{1-loop}}(P^{c+},\ldots,n^{a_{n}+}), \displaystyle\lim_{|1\rangle\to|2\rangle}\mathcal{M}^{\text{1-loop}}(1^{+},2^{+},\ldots,n^{+}) \displaystyle=\text{Split}^{1^{+}2^{+}}_{{\rm G},P^{-}}\mathcal{M}^{\text{1-loop}}(P^{+},\ldots,n^{+}). $$

For one-loop-not-all-plus, the story gets more complicated. We can’t rely on the vanishing of the tree-level-one-minus amplitudes to render the one-loop correction to the 3-pt splitting function zero, as in figure 21. These channels now in fact produce double poles. (In the following section 10 we compute that the one-leg-off-shell-all-plus triangles for gauge theory and gravity are $J_{{\rm YM}+++}^{1{\rm-loop}}\propto\frac{[12]^{2}}{\langle{12}\rangle}$ and $\mathcal{J}_{{\rm G}+++}^{1{\rm-loop}}\propto\frac{[12]^{5}}{\langle{12}\rangle}$ , and multiplying them by the propagator $\frac{i}{\langle{12}\rangle[12]}$ gives the double pole.) These double-poles become important if one wants to compute, say, one-loop-one-minus amplitudes using BCFW recursion [114, 115, 116, 117, 118, 119]. See also [120, 121, 37] for the chiral algebra perspective on the double poles.

We mention that the closely related concept of the “full” collinear limit is defined by taking $p_{1}\to tP$ , $p_{2}\to(1-t)P$ , and $P=p_{1}+p_{2}$ for some constant $t$ . In the full collinear limit we have both $\langle{12}\rangle\to 0$ and $[12]\to 0$ , instead of just $\langle{12}\rangle\to 0$ as in the holomorphic collinear limit. In the full collinear limit, one usually takes $|1\rangle=\sqrt{t}|P\rangle$ , $|1]=\sqrt{t}|P]$ , $|2\rangle=\sqrt{1-t}|P\rangle$ , and $|2]=\sqrt{1-t}|P]$ .

There is also one more type of limit, which we’ll call the “double-scaled” holomorphic collinear limit. This is the limit where $[12]\to 0$ , $\langle{12}\rangle\to 0$ , but $[12]/\langle{12}\rangle\to\infty$ . For real physical momenta, this is equivalent to the full-collinear limit where one then extracts the only terms with a “phase singularity.” This is defined by holding $p_{1}$ fixed and rotating the nearly collinear $p_{2}$ in a tiny circle around it. A remarkable fact about the “double-scaled” holomorphic collinear limit is that its splitting function is uncorrected to all loops in full Einstein gravity. This is however not the case in Yang-Mills theory, as the gravity loop integrals are “softer” than the Yang-Mills loop integrals because the coupling constant $\kappa$ is dimensionful. See for instance section 5.2 of [50] or section 4 of [51].

## 10 Bubbles and triangles

In this section we discuss the loop integrals that arise in SDYM and SDG. This topic will be the subject of a forthcoming paper by the author, Guevara, and Himwich [5]. Here we’ll just be content with looking at the bubble and triangle.

*Figure 23: An $(n^{\prime}\!=\!5)$ -gon*

Consider an $n^{\prime}$ -gon with $n^{\prime}\leq n$ where $n$ is the number of external massless particles. We denote the total off-shell momentum flowing into each leg as $P_{i}$ with $P_{1}+\ldots+P_{n}=0$ . We define the region momenta

$$ P_{1,i}\equiv\sum_{j=1}^{i-1}P_{j} $$

and

$$ P_{i,j}\equiv P_{1,j}-P_{1,i} $$

such that, if $j>i$ ,

$$ P_{i,j}=P_{i}+P_{i+1}+\ldots+P_{j-1}. $$

We parametize the momenta flowing through the diagram via figure 24, where $\ell$ is the loop momentum.

*Figure 24: Momentum flowing through $n^{\prime}$ -gon.*

We regulate the loop diagram using dimensional regularization. We denote as $L$ as the $D=4-2\epsilon$ dimensional momentum we use in the denominator of the diagram while $\ell$ is the $4$ -dimensional part in the numerator. The planar SDYM $n^{\prime}$ -gon is then

$$ \mathcal{I}^{n^{\prime}\text{-gon}}_{\rm SDYM}(P_{1},\ldots,P_{n^{\prime}})=2(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n^{\prime}}\int\!\frac{d^{D}L}{(2\pi)^{D}}\frac{1}{(L+P_{1,1})^{2}\ldots(L+P_{1,n^{\prime}})^{2}}\prod_{i=1}^{n^{\prime}}\langle{\alpha|P_{i}(\ell+P_{1,i})|\alpha}\rangle, $$

and the SDG $n^{\prime}$ -gon is

$$ \mathcal{I}^{n^{\prime}\text{-gon}}_{\rm SDG}(P_{1},\ldots,P_{n^{\prime}})=2\left(-\frac{\kappa}{2}\right)^{n^{\prime}}\int\!\frac{d^{D}L}{(2\pi)^{D}}\frac{1}{(L+P_{1,1})^{2}\ldots(L+P_{1,n^{\prime}})^{2}}\prod_{i=1}^{n^{\prime}}\langle{\alpha|P_{i}(\ell+P_{1,i})|\alpha}\rangle^{2}. $$

There is an overall factor of $2$ for the two orientations of $(+-)$ propagators running around the loop.

In [5] we do the loop integral using standard manipulations and are left with an integral over Feynman parameters. For SDYM, the $n^{\prime}$ -gon is now

$$ \mathcal{I}^{n^{\prime}\text{-gon}}_{\rm SDYM}=2i\frac{(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n^{\prime}}}{(4\pi)^{\frac{D}{2}}}\Gamma\left(n^{\prime}-\tfrac{D}{2}\right)\int_{[0,1]^{n^{\prime}}}d^{n^{\prime}}u\frac{\delta(1-\sum_{k=1}^{n^{\prime}}u_{k})}{(\sum_{r,s}Q_{rs}u_{r}u_{s})^{n^{\prime}-\frac{D}{2}}}\prod_{i=1}^{n^{\prime}}\langle{\alpha|P_{i}\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{n^{\prime}}P_{i,j}u_{j}\Big)|\alpha}\rangle, $$

and for SDG

$$ \mathcal{I}^{n^{\prime}\text{-gon}}_{\rm SDG}=2i\frac{(\kappa/2)^{n^{\prime}}}{(4\pi)^{\frac{D}{2}}}\Gamma\left(n^{\prime}-\tfrac{D}{2}\right)\int_{[0,1]^{n^{\prime}}}d^{n^{\prime}}u\frac{\delta(1-\sum_{k=1}^{n^{\prime}}u_{k})}{(\sum_{r,s}Q_{rs}u_{r}u_{s})^{n^{\prime}-\frac{D}{2}}}\prod_{i=1}^{n^{\prime}}\langle{\alpha|P_{i}\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{n^{\prime}}P_{i,j}u_{j}\Big)|\alpha}\rangle^{2}. $$

Here we have defined the Symanzik matrix

$$ Q_{ij}\equiv\frac{1}{2}(P_{i,j})^{2}. $$

There is much to say about these integrals for general $n^{\prime}$ , but here we’ll just comment on the case of the bubble $n^{\prime}=2$ and the triangle $n^{\prime}=3$ .

While the bubble has a superficial $\Gamma(\epsilon)$ divergence, the numerator

$$ \langle{\alpha|P_{1}(P_{1,1}u_{1}+P_{1,2}u_{2})|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|P_{2}(P_{2,1}u_{1}+P_{2,2}u_{2})|\alpha}\rangle=0 $$

vanishes identically due to $\langle{\alpha|P_{1}P_{1}|\alpha}\rangle=0$ . Therefore, the SDYM and SDG bubbles vanish in dimensional regularization, even when $P_{1}$ is off-shell.44 4 In other schemes however the bubble does not vanish identically, see for instance [122, 123, 124, 125, 126].

*Figure 25: The bubble diagram vanishes in SDYM and SDG in dim-reg.*

Now we look at the triangle with two legs on-shell, i.e. $P_{1}=p_{1}$ , $P_{2}=p_{2}$ with $p_{1}^{2}=p_{2}^{2}=0$ and $P_{3}=-P_{1}-P_{2}$ .

*Figure 26: Triangle diagram with $p_{1}^{2}=p_{2}^{2}=0$ for computing $\mathcal{J}_{+++}^{\text{1-loop}}.$*

We will now define the SDYM and SDG one-loop-all-plus 3-pt currents via

$$ \displaystyle J_{{\rm YM}+++}^{1{\rm-loop}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{2}}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{2}}\mathcal{I}^{3-{\rm gon}}_{\rm SDYM}, \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{{\rm G}+++}^{1{\rm-loop}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{4}}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{4}}\mathcal{I}^{3-{\rm gon}}_{\rm SDG}. $$

In order to compute the one-loop-all-plus three-point currents all we have to do is use (170) and (171). We will also denote the measure of the integral over the simplex as $\int_{\Delta_{3}}\equiv\int_{[0,1]^{3}}d^{3}u\delta(1\!-\!u_{1}\!-\!u_{2}\!-\!u_{3})$ for brevity. For SDYM,

$$ \displaystyle J_{{\rm YM}+++}^{1{\rm-loop}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{2}}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{2}}2i\frac{(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{3}}{(4\pi)^{2}}\int_{\Delta_{3}}\frac{(\langle{\alpha|12|\alpha}\rangle u_{3})(\langle{\alpha|23|\alpha}\rangle u_{1})(\langle{\alpha|31|\alpha}\rangle u_{1})}{(p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}u_{1}u_{3}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{2}}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{2}}2i\frac{(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{3}}{(4\pi)^{2}}\frac{1}{6}\langle{\alpha|12|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|23|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|31|\alpha}\rangle\frac{1}{\langle{12}\rangle[12]} \displaystyle=-i\frac{(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{3}}{3(4\pi)^{2}}\langle\alpha 1\rangle\langle\alpha 2\rangle\frac{[12]^{2}}{\langle{12}\rangle} $$

and for SDG

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{{\rm G}+++}^{1{\rm-loop}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{4}}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{4}}2i\frac{(\kappa/2)^{3}}{(4\pi)^{2}}\int_{\Delta_{3}}\frac{(\langle{\alpha|12|\alpha}\rangle u_{3})^{2}(\langle{\alpha|23|\alpha}\rangle u_{1})^{2}(\langle{\alpha|31|\alpha}\rangle u_{1})^{2}}{(p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}u_{1}u_{3}} \displaystyle=2i\frac{(\kappa/2)^{3}}{(4\pi)^{2}}\frac{1}{360}\frac{[12]^{5}\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{2}}{\langle{12}\rangle}. $$

Here we have used the particular simplex integrals

$$ \displaystyle\int_{\Delta_{3}}\,u_{1}=\frac{1}{6}, \displaystyle\int_{\Delta_{3}}\,u_{1}u_{2}^{2}u_{3}=\frac{1}{360}. $$

If we wish to compute the 3-pt one-loop-all-plus amplitudes, we simply put the third leg on-shell. This gives

$$ \displaystyle A_{3;1}^{1{\rm-loop}}(1^{+},2^{+},3^{+})=\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 3}\rangle^{2}}J_{{\rm YM}+++}^{{1{\rm-loop}}}\Big\rvert_{p_{3}^{2}=0} \displaystyle=0 \displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{1{\rm-loop}}(1^{+},2^{+},3^{+})=\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 3}\rangle^{4}}\mathcal{J}_{{\rm G}+++}^{{1{\rm-loop}}}\Big\rvert_{p_{3}^{2}=0} \displaystyle=0 $$

where here we used $P_{3}^{2}=p_{3}^{2}=[12]\langle{12}\rangle$ . These amplitudes are considered to vanish because there are more powers of $[12]$ in the numerator than $\langle{12}\rangle$ in the denominator. (The subscript in $A_{3;1}^{1{\rm-loop}}$ denotes that this is the single-trace part of the amplitude, although at 3-pts this is also the full amplitude because $\Tr(T^a)=0$ for $T^{a}\in\mathfrak{su}(N_{c})$ .)

Other works which study SDYM and SDG loop integrals include [72, 127, 126, 128] and the papers of Chakrabarti, Qiu, and Thorn [123, 124, 125].

## 11 Double-off-shell calculation of one-loop-all-plus amplitudes

### 11.1 SDYM double-off-shell current calculation

In this section we will review a historical computation and compute an all- $n$ closed form expression for the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes in Yang-Mills theory. This expression was conjectured in [129, 130] because it had the correct collinear and soft limits, and was proven by Mahlon in [75, 76] using the recursive currents techniques we review here.

In particular, Mahlon computed the “double-off-shell-current” of tree-level diagrams with an arbitrary number of on-shell positive-helicity gluons and two off-shell quarks. The off-shell quark legs can then be sewn together and integrated over to give the contribution to one-loop-all-plus gluon QCD amplitudes where an internal massless quark is running around the loop. From supersymmetry, one can deduce that the full one-loop-all-plus amplitude is proportional to $(1+\tfrac{N_{s}}{N_{c}}-\tfrac{N_{f}}{N_{c}})$ , where $N_{f}$ is the number of internal quarks running around the loop and $N_{s}$ is the number of internal complex scalars. Therefore, Mahlon’s result is $-\frac{N_{f}}{N_{c}}$ times the one-loop-all-plus amplitude in pure YM. With his double-off-shell current, Mahlon also computed many other other families of amplitudes, including the one-loop-one-minus amplitudes.

In this section, we will work in pure SDYM, translating Mahlon’s quark-loop calculation into a pure gluon-loop calculation. We use the Feynman rules from the scalar SDYM lightcone action, and this slightly simplifies the calculation.

We denote the color-ordered55 5 By color-ordered, we mean we are restricting ourselves to planar Feynman diagrams where the external momenta $\ell$ , $1,\ldots,n,m$ are fixed in a clockwise pattern around the diagram, as in figure 27. See appendix C or eq. (121) for the analogous equation with single-off-shell currents. all-plus double-off-shell current by $J_{\rm YM}(\ell\,;1,\ldots,n)$ . $\ell$ is an off-shell momentum with $\ell^{2}\neq 0$ , while $p_{1}^{2}=\ldots=p_{n}^{2}=0$ . Diagrammatically, $\ell$ , $1,\ldots,n$ are all positive-helicity. (We are able to assign helicity to particles which are off-shell because we are working in lightcone gauge.) There is a second off-shell negative-helicity particle called $m$ , where $p_{m}\equiv-(\ell+p_{1}+\ldots+p_{n})$ . The off-shell legs are of course not given polarization factors, while the on-shell legs are. We also include the propagator factors $i/\ell^{2}$ and $i/p_{m}^{2}$ for the off-shell legs. See figure 27.

*Figure 27: Color-ordered all-plus double-off-shell current definition.*

The base case for the double-off-shell current is simply

$$ J_{\rm YM}(\ell)=\frac{i}{\ell^{2}}. $$

Compare this to the analogous formula for the on-shell case, $J_{\rm YM}(i)=\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}}$ , which includes a polarization factor.

We remind the reader of the formula for the single-off-shell-all-plus current that was given in eq. (125), which we reproduce below.

$$ J_{\rm YM}(1,\ldots,n)=(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n-1}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle}\frac{1}{\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n-1,n}\rangle}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle} $$

We can now create a Berends-Giele recursion relation for the double-off-shell current by gluing lower-point double-off-shell and single-off-shell currents together. See figure fig 28.

*Figure 28: Double-off-shell current recursion relation (181).*

The equation for this recursion relation is

$$ (\ell+p_{N})^{2}J_{\rm YM}(\ell\,;N)=i\sqrt{2}g\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=0\\
A=\{1,\ldots,j\}\\
B=\{j+1,\ldots,n\}\end{subarray}}^{n-1}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{A})p_{B}|\alpha}\rangle J_{\rm YM}(\ell\,;A)J_{\rm YM}(B) $$

where we define the ordered set $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ . We now give the scalar lightcone gluon version of Mahlon’s solution for this current.

$$ \boxed{J_{\rm YM}(\ell\,;\,1,\ldots,n)=(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n}\frac{-i}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n-1,n}\rangle\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,j})j|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,j-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,j})^{2}}\right)} $$

We prove this formula satisfies the recursion relation in appendix F.1. Here we use the notation66 6 In terms of our region momenta from the previous section 10, $p_{i,j}=P_{i,j+1}$ .

$$ p_{i,j}\equiv p_{i}+p_{i+1}+\ldots+p_{j-1}+p_{j} $$

where we also define

$$ p_{i,i-1}\equiv 0. $$

It is easy to check that in the limit that $\ell^{2}\to 0$ , the double-off-shell-current becomes the single-off-shell current, modulo the dropped polarization factor and the extra propagator:

$$ \lim_{\ell^{2}\to 0}(\tfrac{\ell^{2}}{i})J_{\rm YM}(\ell\,;\,1,\ldots,n)=\langle{\alpha\ell}\rangle^{2}J_{\rm YM}(\ell,1,\ldots,n)\Big\rvert_{\ell^{2}=0}. $$

Note that the closed-form-solution (182) only has two propagators in the denominator instead of the $n$ propagators one would naively expect from the Feynman diagrams.

In principle we should be able to sew together the two off-shell legs of this current and integrate over the loop momentum $\ell$ in order to compute the one-loop-all-plus amplitude.

However, if we want to regulate our loop integral using dimensional regularization, then our loop momentum does not live in 4 dimensions but rather in $4-2\epsilon$ dimensions, and this modifies the double-off-shell current. We denote our $4-2\epsilon$ dimensional vector as $L$ , for which $\ell$ is its 4 dimensional component. The norm $L^{2}$ can then be expressed as

$$ L^{2}=\ell^{2}-\mu^{2} $$

where $\mu^{2}$ is the magnitude of the $-2\epsilon$ dimensional part orthogonal to the 4 dimensional part. (The minus sign in front of $\mu^{2}$ is because we are working in mostly minus signature.) We also have

$$ (L+p)^{2}=(\ell+p)^{2}-\mu^{2} $$

if $p$ is some other 4 dimensional vector.

In our dimensional regularization scheme, we replace all the propagators in the denominators of our Feynman diagrams $i/\ell^{2}$ with $i/L^{2}$ . The numerators, however, do not get modified. They remain living in exactly $4$ dimensions, i.e. they depend on $\ell$ and not $L$ . This means that the recursion relation for the double-off-shell current (181) should have $((\ell+p_{N})^{2}-\mu^{2})$ on the LHS instead of $(\ell+p_{N})^{2}$ .

This regularization modifies the double-off shell current. It becomes

$$ \displaystyle J_{\rm YM}(L\, \displaystyle;1,\ldots,n)=(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n}\frac{-i}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n-1,n}\rangle\langle{\alpha n}\rangle} \displaystyle\times\sum_{j=1}^{n}\Bigg(\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,j})j|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{1,j-1})^{2}(L+p_{1,j})^{2}}-\mu^{2}\frac{\langle{\alpha|p_{j,n}j|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{1,j-1})^{2}(L+p_{1,j})^{2}(L+p_{1,n})^{2}}\Bigg). $$

$$  $$

We prove the above formula in appendix F.2. Let us briefly describe where the $\mu^{2}$ corrected term comes from. In the proof of the formula for the 4-dimensional double-off-shell current, one uses a certain Clifford algebra identity that re-expresses expressions roughly like $\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p)\ldots|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p)\ldots|\alpha}\rangle$ into terms roughly like $(\ell+p)^{2}(\ldots)$ . These terms then cancel propagators in the denominator. However, with the regulated denominators, these numerators and denominators will no longer cancel exactly, and we in particular have the relation

$$ \frac{(\ell+p)^{2}}{(L+p)^{2}}=1+\frac{\mu^{2}}{(L+p)^{2}}. $$

The above identity is the source of the correction term in (188).

Actually, (188) is not the fully corrected formula, but for the purposes of computing the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes it is the only part which contributes after integration. (188) is more precisely what one gets by going up exactly “one-level” in the recursive formula (181). In other words, one obtains this formula for $J_{\rm YM}(L\,;\,N)$ by modifying the propagator $(\ell+p_{N})^{2}\to(L+p_{N})^{2}$ on the LHS of (181), using the naive 4 dimensional formula for $J_{\rm YM}(\ell\,;\,A)$ (182) on the RHS while simply shifting $\ell\to L$ in its denominator. We’ll explain why this is sufficient in a bit.

*Figure 29: Configuration of currents necessary to compute one-loop-all-plus SDYM amplitudes. We need to glue a single-off-shell-all-plus current to a double-off-shell-all-plus current in order to have all the correct tree configurations. If we just glued the double-off-shell current to itself, particle $1$ couldn’t have any particles to the left of it in its tree in the color ordered diagram and $n$ couldn’t have any particles to the right of it.*

In order to compute the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes, we want to sew the two off-shell legs together and integrate over $L$ . However there is a slight issue we must address about color ordering. Note that all one-loop diagrams take the form of trees pasted on a central loop. If we were to just glue the $L$ and $m$ legs together, the color ordered trees we sum over from figure 27 will always have particle $1$ on the leftmost side of a tree and particle $n$ on the rightmost side of a tree. You would never get $1$ or $n$ in the middle of a tree, which is a problem. We need to find a way to fix this by hand. We can accomplish this by gluing the single-off-shell current to the double off-shell current, as shown in figure 29, where we take particle $1$ to always belong to this tree.

This means that the single-trace part of the one-loop-all-plus amplitude is given by

$$ A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n;1}=-2\int\frac{d^{D}L}{(2\pi)^{D}}\sum_{1\leq y<z\leq n}\sqrt{2}g\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{y+1,z}|\alpha}\rangle J_{\rm YM}(z\!+\!1,\ldots,y)J_{\rm YM}(L\,;y\!+\!1,\ldots,z). $$

The factor of 2 is for the two directions the $(+-)$ propagators can flow through the loop and the overall sign is due to the direction of momentum flow through the diagram.

Let us now explain our chosen loop integration scheme. We use dimensional regularization with

$$ D=4-2\epsilon $$

and split the integration measure up using

$$ \int\frac{d^{D}L}{(2\pi)^{D}}=\int\frac{d^{4}\ell}{(2\pi)^{4}}\int\frac{d^{-2\epsilon}\mu}{(2\pi)^{-2\epsilon}}. $$

We now begin massaging (190). We define the Parke-Taylor factor

$$ \text{PT}\equiv\langle{12}\rangle\langle{23}\rangle\ldots\langle{n-1,n}\rangle\langle{n1}\rangle $$

for economy. We then have

$$ \displaystyle A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n;1}=-\frac{2(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n}}{\text{PT}}\int\frac{d^{D}L}{(2\pi)^{D}}\sum_{1\leq y<z\leq n}\frac{\langle{y,y+1}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha y}\rangle\langle{\alpha,y+1}\rangle}\frac{\langle{z,z+1}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha z}\rangle\langle{\alpha,z+1}\rangle}\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{y+1,z}|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle\times\Bigg(\sum_{j=y+1}^{z}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{y+1,j})j|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{y+1,j-1})^{2}(L+p_{y+1,j})^{2}}-\mu^{2}\sum_{j=y+1}^{z}\frac{\langle{\alpha|p_{j,z}j|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{y+1,j-1})^{2}(L+p_{y+1,j})^{2}(L+p_{y+1,z})^{2}}\Bigg). $$

Let’s start by integrating the first term, which is naively divergent by power counting. Shfting the integration measure, we have

$$ \int\frac{d^{D}L}{(2\pi)^{D}}\frac{\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{y+1,z}|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{y+1,j})j|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{y+1,j-1})^{2}(L+p_{y+1,j})^{2}}=\int\frac{d^{D}L}{(2\pi)^{D}}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell-p_{y+1,j-1})p_{y+1,z}|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|\ell j|\alpha}\rangle}{L^{2}(L+p_{j})^{2}}=0. $$

It is relatively straightforward to see that the above integral is zero due to a few standard identities. In order to evaluate this integral, one introduces a Feynman paramater to shift $\ell$ on the RHS by a vector proportional to $p_{j}$ in order to complete the square in the denominator. One then uses

$$ \displaystyle\int\frac{d^{4}\ell^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{4}}\int\frac{d^{-2\epsilon}\mu}{(2\pi)^{-2\epsilon}}\frac{{\ell^{\prime}}^{\nu}}{({\ell^{\prime}}^{2}-\Delta-\mu^{2})^{3}} \displaystyle=0 \displaystyle\int\frac{d^{4}\ell^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{4}}\int\frac{d^{-2\epsilon}\mu}{(2\pi)^{-2\epsilon}}\frac{{\ell^{\prime}}^{\nu}{\ell^{\prime}}^{\rho}}{({\ell^{\prime}}^{2}-\Delta-\mu^{2})^{3}} \displaystyle\propto\eta^{\nu\rho}. $$

where $\ell^{\prime}$ is the momentum after the Feynman parameter shift. Note that these formulae follow simply from the index structures of the integrands. The part quadratic in $\ell^{\prime}$ , which naively would have been the most divergent piece, vanishes after integration because it appears in the structure $\langle{\alpha|\ell^{\prime}\ldots|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|\ell^{\prime}\ldots|\alpha}\rangle$ , and from the Fierz identity $\eta^{\nu\rho}\sigma_{\nu A\dot{A}}\sigma_{\rho B\dot{B}}=2\varepsilon_{AB}\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}$ it is zero because $\langle{\alpha\alpha}\rangle=0$ .

So, the naively divergent first “bubble” term in (194) is zero. Now let us turn to the $\mu^{2}$ corrected “triangle” term. We introduce Feynman parameters to put it in standard form. We use the identity

$$ \displaystyle\frac{1}{(L+p_{y+1,j-1})^{2}(L+p_{y+1,j})^{2}(L+p_{y+1,z})^{2}} \displaystyle=2!\int_{[0,1]^{3}}d^{3}u\frac{\delta(1\!-\!u_{1}\!-\!u_{2}\!-\!u_{3})}{(u_{1}(L+p_{y+1,j-1})^{2}+u_{2}(L+p_{y+1,j})^{2}+u_{3}(L+p_{y+1,z})^{2})^{3}} $$

and foil out the denominator, finding it to be

$$ \displaystyle(\ell^{2}+2\ell\cdot(u_{1}p_{y+1,j-1}+u_{2}p_{y+1,j}+u_{3}p_{y+1,z})+u_{1}p_{y+1,j-1}^{2}+u_{2}p_{y+1,j}^{2}+u_{3}p_{y+1,z}^{2}-\mu^{2})^{3}. $$

Now we do the shift

$$ \ell=\ell^{\prime}-u_{1}p_{y+1,j-1}-u_{2}p_{y+1,j}-u_{3}p_{y+1,z} $$

to complete the square, finding that the denominator is now

$$ ({L^{\prime}}^{2}-\Delta)^{3} $$

where $\Delta=(u_{1}p_{y+1,j-1}+u_{2}p_{y+1,j}^{2}+u_{3}p_{y+1,z})^{2}-u_{1}p_{y+1,j-1}^{2}-u_{2}p_{y+1,j}^{2}-u_{3}p_{y+1,z}^{2}$ . We now have

$$ \displaystyle A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n;1} \displaystyle=\frac{2(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n}}{\text{PT}}\sum_{1\leq y<z\leq n}\frac{\langle{y,y+1}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha y}\rangle\langle{\alpha,y+1}\rangle}\frac{\langle{z,z+1}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha z}\rangle\langle{\alpha,z+1}\rangle} \displaystyle\times 2!\int_{[0,1]^{3}}d^{3}u\,\delta(1\!-\!u_{1}\!-\!u_{2}\!-\!u_{3})\sum_{j=y+1}^{z}\langle{\alpha|p_{j,z}j|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle\times\int\frac{d^{D}L^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{D}}\frac{\mu^{2}}{({L^{\prime}}^{2}-\Delta)^{3}}\langle{\alpha|(\cancel{\ell^{\prime}}-u_{1}p_{y+1,j-1}-u_{2}p_{y+1,j}-u_{3}\cancel{p_{y+1,z}})p_{y+1,z}|\alpha}\rangle. $$

The first cancelled-out term vanishes because the $\ell^{\prime}$ integrand is odd. The second cancelled-out term vanishes from $\langle{\alpha|p_{y+1,z}p_{y+1,z}|\alpha}\rangle=0$ .

The question now becomes, how do we perform the loop integral which has an inserted factor of $\mu^{2}$ ? We will now explain how, following appendix A of [131].

$\mu^{2}$ is the $-2\epsilon$ dimensional magnitude of $L^{2}$ which is orthogonal to the 4 dimensional part. Note that it is in a spatial direction and not the time direction. We can consider the symbol $\mu$ to be the radial magnitude with $\mu\geq 0$ . Furthermore we recall that the general expression for the angular integral of the unit $d$ -sphere $S_{d}$ is

$$ \int d\Omega_{d}=\frac{2\pi^{\frac{d+1}{2}}}{\Gamma(\frac{d+1}{2})}. $$

Consider an integral over some function of the form $f(\ell^{\nu},\mu^{2})$ along with an insertion $(\mu^{2})^{r}$ for some $r$ . This insertion changes the radial phase space factor for the integration over $\mu$ , shifting the dimension $4-2\epsilon\to 4+2r-2\epsilon$ . Accounting for the difference in the angular phase space factor then multiplies the expression by a factor proportional to $\epsilon$ :

$$ \displaystyle\int\frac{d^{4-2\epsilon}L}{(2\pi)^{4-2\epsilon}}(\mu^{2})^{r}f(\ell^{\nu},\mu^{2}) \displaystyle=\int\frac{d^{4}\ell}{(2\pi)^{4}}\int\frac{d^{-2\epsilon}\mu}{(2\pi)^{-2\epsilon}}(\mu^{2})^{r}f(\ell^{\nu},\mu^{2}) \displaystyle=\int\frac{d^{4}\ell}{(2\pi)^{4}}\int d\Omega_{-1-2\epsilon}\int_{0}^{\infty}d\mu\,\mu^{-1-2\epsilon}\,(\mu^{2})^{r}f(\ell^{\nu},\mu^{2}) \displaystyle=(2\pi)^{2r}\frac{\int d\Omega_{-1-2\epsilon}}{\int d\Omega_{-1-2\epsilon+2r}}\int\frac{d^{4}\ell}{(2\pi)^{4}}\int\frac{d^{-2\epsilon+2r}\mu}{(2\pi)^{-2\epsilon+2r}}f(\ell^{\nu},\mu^{2}) \displaystyle=-\epsilon(1-\epsilon)\ldots(r-1-\epsilon)(4\pi)^{r}\int\frac{d^{4+2r-2\epsilon}L}{(2\pi)^{4+2r-2\epsilon}}f(\ell^{\nu},\mu^{2}). $$

Using the well-known scalar loop integral

$$ \int\!\frac{d^{D}L^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{D}}\frac{1}{({L^{\prime}}^{2}-\Delta)^{a}}=i\frac{(-1)^{a}}{(4\pi)^{\frac{D}{2}}}\frac{1}{\Delta^{a-\frac{D}{2}}}\frac{\Gamma(a-\frac{D}{2})}{\Gamma(a)} $$

our desired integral in (201) becomes a triangle in $6-2\epsilon$ dimensions, and the dimension shifting extracts a single finite piece after a $\epsilon/\epsilon$ cancellation:

$$ \int\frac{d^{4-2\epsilon}L^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{4-2\epsilon}}\frac{\mu^{2}}{({L^{\prime}}^{2}-\Delta)^{3}}=-\epsilon\,(4\pi)\int\frac{d^{6-2\epsilon}L^{\prime}}{(2\pi)^{6-2\epsilon}}\frac{1}{({L^{\prime}}^{2}-\Delta)^{3}}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{i}{(4\pi)^{2}}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon). $$

Before proceeding, let us comment on a previous point we did not justify at the time. The $4-2\epsilon$ dimensional double-off-shell current is supposed to be a solution to the full $4-2\epsilon$ dimensional recursion, i.e. the relation where one replaces $(\ell+p_{N})^{2}\mapsto(L+p_{N})^{2}$ on the LHS of (181). However our actual expression (188) came from going up just “one step” in the recursive formula, where one takes the naive 4-dimensional expression for $J_{\rm YM}(\ell;A)$ and simply replaces its denominators $(\ell+p)^{2}\mapsto(L+p)^{2}$ . We now explain why this procedure is sufficient. Note that we can calculate further corrections to the formula recursively by re-plugging in our $\mu^{2}$ -corrected solution into the recursive formula over and over. Let us label all terms in the corrected current by $(r,a)$ , where $r$ is the power of $(\mu^{2})^{r}$ in the term and $a$ is the number of propagators. So (188) for instance has a $(0,2)$ term and a $(1,3)$ term. (The number of $\ell$ ’s in the numerator won’t affect the divergence of the $L$ integrals because after shifting by Feynman parameters they all go away due to $\langle{\alpha\alpha}\rangle=0$ , so we don’t have to keep track of them in the label.) As we recursively plug our formula into the Berends-Giele recursive formula, each subsequent step will create a term with an extra propagator due to the final division by $(L+p_{N})^{2}$ . The next correction, for instance, will be of the form $(1,4)$ . All other subsequent corrections will also be of the form $(r,a)$ for $r<a-2$ . (At any stage, it could be the case that a Clifford algebra identity could create an $(\ell+p)^{2}$ in the numerator, which could cancel and produce a $1+\frac{\mu^{2}}{(L+p)^{2}}$ , but note that this will not modify the previous statement.) However, from (204) we can see that the corresponding loop integrals with $D=4+2r-2\epsilon$ are finite and are killed by the overall $\epsilon$ for $r<a-2$ , so these extra corrections won’t contribute.

We now plug our triangle integral (205) back into (201). We also use the simplex integral

$$ \int_{[0,1]^{3}}d^{3}u\,\delta(1\!-\!u_{1}\!-\!u_{2}\!-\!u_{3})u_{i}=\frac{1}{6} $$

to get a closed-form expression just in terms of spinor helicity variables,

$$ \displaystyle A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n;1}=-\frac{i}{3(4\pi)^{2}}\frac{(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n}}{\text{PT}} \displaystyle\sum_{1\leq y<j\leq z\leq n}\frac{\langle{y,y+1}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha y}\rangle\langle{\alpha,y+1}\rangle}\frac{\langle{z,z+1}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha z}\rangle\langle{\alpha,z+1}\rangle} \displaystyle\times\langle{\alpha|p_{j,z}j|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|(p_{y+1,j-1}+p_{y+1,j})p_{y+1,z}|\alpha}\rangle. $$

We could certainly at this point use standard tricks to further transform this expression, but we contented ourselves with simply checking numerically on a computer to high multiplicity that, with momentum conservation, it is equal to

$$ \boxed{A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n;1}=-\frac{i}{3}\frac{(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n}}{(4\pi)^{2}}\frac{1}{\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n1}\rangle}\sum_{1\leq i_{1}<i_{2}<i_{3}<i_{4}\leq n}\langle{i_{1}i_{2}}\rangle[i_{2}i_{3}]\langle{i_{3}i_{4}}\rangle[i_{4}i_{1}].} $$

Note that the expression is rational and does not depend on the reference spinor $|\alpha\rangle$ , as promised.

The full amplitude can be written as a sum of single-trace partial amplitudes and double-trace partial amplitudes via

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{\text{1-loop}}(1,\ldots,n)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}/\mathbb{Z}_{n}}N_{c}\tr(T^{\sigma(1)} \ldots T^{\sigma(n)} )A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n;1}(\sigma(1),\ldots,\sigma(n)) \displaystyle+\sum_{j=2}^{\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor+1}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}/\mathbb{Z}_{j-1}\times\mathbb{Z}_{n-j+1}}\tr(T^{\sigma(1) } \ldots T^{\sigma(j-1)})\tr(T^{\sigma(j)} \ldots T^{\sigma(n)})A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n;j}(\sigma(1)\ldots\sigma(n)). $$

We review one-loop color ordering in more detail in appendix C. The point we want to make here is that the double-trace partial amplitudes are uniquely determined by the single-trace partial amplitudes via

$$ A_{n;j}^{\text{1-loop}}(1,2,\ldots,j\!-\!1;j,\ldots,n)=(-1)^{j-1}\sum_{\sigma\in\text{COP}\{\alpha\}\{\beta\}}A_{n;1}^{\text{1-loop}}(\sigma(1),\ldots,\sigma(n)) $$

where “ $\text{COP}\{\alpha\}\{\beta\}$ ” is a certain set of color-ordered-permutation we again define in appendix C. From the above formula and (208), one can check the following closed-form expression for the double-trace terms of the one-loop-all-plus amplitude holds: [132, 133]

$$ A_{n;j}^{\text{1-loop}}=-2i\frac{(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n}}{(4\pi)^{2}}\frac{(p_{1,j-1}^{2})^{2}}{(\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{j-1,1}\rangle)(\langle{j,j+1}\rangle\ldots\langle{nj}\rangle)}. $$

### 11.2 SDG double-off-shell current calculation

Let us look at the analogous calculation for gravity. The authors BDPR [50] presented an expression for the double-off-shell SDG current in appendix B of their paper without proof. The 4-dimensional double-off-shell current satisfies the recursion relation

$$ (\ell+p_{N})^{2}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(\ell\,;\,N)=-\frac{\kappa}{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\cup B=N\\
A\cap B=\emptyset,B\neq\emptyset\end{subarray}}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{A})p_{B}|\alpha}\rangle^{2}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(\ell\,;\,A)\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(B) $$

and, with our conventions, is determined by the base case

$$ \mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(\ell)=\frac{i}{\ell^{2}}. $$

The closed-form expression is given by

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(\ell\,;\,N)= \displaystyle\frac{(\kappa/2)^{n}(-i)}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n\!-\!1,n}\rangle\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,j})j|\alpha}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha j}\rangle^{2}}\right)\left(\sum_{m=1}^{n}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,m})m|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,m-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,m})^{2}}\right) \displaystyle+\mathcal{P}(1,2,\ldots,n). $$

Here $\mathcal{P}(1,2,\ldots,n)$ is a sum over all permutations of the elements $1,2,\ldots,n$ . If one takes $\ell^{2}\to 0$ on-shell, amputates the $\ell$ propagator and accounts for the overall polarization factors, the double-off-shell current becomes equal to the single-off-shell current:

$$ \lim_{\ell^{2}\to 0}(\tfrac{\ell^{2}}{i})\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(\ell;1,\ldots,n)=\langle{\alpha\ell}\rangle^{4}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(\ell,1,\ldots,n)\Big\rvert_{\ell^{2}=0}. $$

The $4-2\epsilon$ -dimensional double-off-shell current is defined by going one stage up in the recursion relation, continuing all the denominators to $4-2\epsilon$ dimensions while keeping the numerators in $4$ dimensions:

$$ \mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(L\,;\,N)\equiv\frac{-\kappa/2}{(L+p_{N})^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\cup B=N\\
A\cap B=\emptyset,B\neq\emptyset\end{subarray}}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{A})p_{B}|\alpha}\rangle^{2}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(\ell\,;\,A)\Big\rvert_{\ell\,\mapsto L}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(B). $$

BDPR provide an expression for this current as well. It is

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(L\,;\,N) \displaystyle=\frac{(\kappa/2)^{n}(-i)}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n\!-\!1,n}\rangle\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{n}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,j})j|\alpha}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha j}\rangle^{2}}\right) \displaystyle\times\sum_{m=1}^{n}\frac{1}{(L+p_{1,m-1})^{2}(L+p_{1,m})^{2}}\left[\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,m})m|\alpha}\rangle-\frac{\mu^{2}}{(L+p_{1,n})^{2}}\langle{\alpha|p_{m,n}m|\alpha}\rangle\right] \displaystyle+\mathcal{P}(1,2,\ldots,n). $$

In their paper, they claim that they numerically checked the 4-dimensional current up to $n=8$ , and checked the $\mu^{2}$ -correction up to $n=3$ . We have numerically checked the full current, including the $\mu^{2}$ -correction, up to $n=10$ by generating random values for all the momenta and $\mu^{2}$ .

The formula (217) of course does not look like the tree formula for the single-off-shell current. There is almost certainly a nicer formula for $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(L;N)$ which generalizes the tree formula in some direct way. It would be interesting to find this expression.

Armed with the formula for the double-off-shell current, we can use it to compute an all-multiplicity expression for the one-loop-all-plus gravity amplitudes. This computation was sketched in words in [50] and we are told the authors performed the computation for $n=4,5$ , but here we carry it out to all $n$ . Note we cannot simply glue the two off-shell legs together due to an issue with overcounting. For instance, the configurations with $r$ trees coming off the central loop will be overcounted by a factor of $r$ because said trees can be cycled around the loop. To fix this issue, we have to glue a single-off-shell current containing one particular particle, say particle 1, to the double-off-shell vertex. The configuration is analogous to what we used in the Yang-Mills case in figure 29. Here, we sum over all the non-empty subsets $A$ and $B$ such that $A\cup B=N$ and $1\in B$ . We then attach the single-off-shell current $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(B)$ to the double-off-shell current $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(L;A)$ :

$$ \mathcal{M}^{\text{1-loop}}(1^{+},\ldots,n^{+})=\frac{i\kappa}{2}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\cup B=N\\
A\cap B=\emptyset\\
1\in B,A\neq\emptyset\end{subarray}}\int\frac{d^{D}L}{(2\pi)^{D}}\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{B}|\alpha}\rangle^{2}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(L;A)\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(B). $$

(An overall factor of 2 for the orientations of the $(+-)$ propagators is cancelled by a $1/2$ for graph-reflection symmetry after the currents are glued.) Using this expression, it is easy to introduce Feynman parameters and do the loop integrals exactly as we did in SDYM. The 4-dimensional “bubble” piece can immediately be seen to vanish due to the numerator structure. Only the $\mu^{2}$ -corrected triangle piece remains, and any term with an $\langle\alpha|\ell^{\prime}\ldots$ after the Feynman parameter shift vanishes. Only a simple scalar triangle integral in $6-2\epsilon$ dimensions remains which we already computed in (205). The final result is

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{M}^{\text{1-loop}}(1^{+},\ldots,n^{+})=\frac{-i\kappa/2}{(4\pi)^{2}} \displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}A\cup B=N\\
A\cap B=\emptyset\\
1\in B,A\neq\emptyset\end{subarray}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{all possible}\\
\text{permutations}\\
\text{of }A\text{ in }\mathcal{P}(A)\end{subarray}}\sum_{m=1}^{|A|}\int_{[0,1]^{3}}d^{3}u\,\delta(1\!-\!u_{1}\!-\!u_{2}\!-\!u_{3}) \displaystyle\times\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(B)\langle{\alpha|(u_{1}p_{A}+u_{2}p_{a_{1},a_{m-1}}+u_{3}p_{a_{1},a_{m}})p_{B}|\alpha}\rangle^{2} \displaystyle\times\frac{(\kappa/2)^{|A|}}{\langle{\alpha a_{1}}\rangle\langle{a_{1}a_{2}}\rangle\ldots\langle{a_{|A|-1}a_{|A|}}\rangle\langle{\alpha a_{|A|}}\rangle}\langle{\alpha|p_{a_{m}a_{|A|}}a_{m}|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle\times\prod_{j=1}^{|A|}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(-u_{1}p_{A}-u_{2}p_{a_{1},a_{m-1}}-u_{3}p_{a_{1},a_{m}}+p_{a_{1},a_{j}})a_{j}|\alpha}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha a_{j}}\rangle^{2}}. $$

Note that we have not performed the trivial integrals over Feynman parameters. They are given by $\int_{[0,1]^{3}}d^{3}u\delta(1\!-\!u_{1}\!-\!u_{2}\!-\!u_{3})u_{1}^{n_{1}}u_{2}^{n_{2}}u_{3}^{n_{3}}=n_{1}!n_{2}!n_{3}!/(2+n_{1}+n_{2}+n_{3})!$ , but we haven’t executed this above because it would make the formula more complicated.

Admittedly, the above formula is a bit less than inspiring, but it is at least a closed form expression for the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes that can be derived using Feynman diagrammatics.

An interesting point is that the above expression can easily be transformed into an expression for the one-loop-one-minus amplitudes if one replaces the all-plus current $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(B)$ with the one-minus current we could denote by $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1^{-},(B-\{1\})^{+})$ :

$$ \mathcal{M}^{\text{1-loop}}(1^{-},2^{+},\ldots,n^{+})=\eqref{1141}\big\rvert_{\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(B)\,\mapsto\,\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1^{-},(B-\{1\})^{+})}. $$

An all-multiplicity solution for the one-minus current was recently found by Hasuwannakit and Krasnov [93], which means that there does now exist an all multiplicity expression for the one-loop-one-minus gravity amplitudes.

## 12 Unitarity cuts in $D$ dimensions

In this section we will give a cursory overview of the unitarity method for computing one-loop-all-plus amplitudes [134, 131, 135]. In particular, we compute the 4-pt one-loop-all-plus SDYM amplitude with this method.

It is well known that unitarity (the optical theorem) implies that the discontinuities of a one-loop amplitude are given by the on-shell cuts of the amplitude. Furthermore, as discussed in section 9.1, all the cuts of the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes are zero, meaning the amplitudes are rational. So, given that the cuts are zero, how could we possibly use cuts to compute these amplitudes? The answer is that, while all of the 4-dimensional cuts are zero, the $D=4-2\epsilon$ dimensional cuts are not zero! Strictly speaking, however, it does not make sense to talk about $4-2\epsilon$ dimensional cuts using standard unitarity theorems. This method should more precisely be thought of as a way to construct simplified ansatze for Feynman integrands. In its modern incarnation, one typically performs four cuts, specifying the four components of the loop momentum, and turns any loop into a sum of boxes, triangles, and bubbles. This is of course even more remote from actual unitarity and is therefore referred to as “generalized unitarity.” For a description of the modern method, see for instance the work of Badger [136, 110]. See also for instance the discussion in [72]. Here however we will stick to the old-fashioned method based on two-particle cuts.

The method essentially boils down to constructing Feynman integrals which have all the correct cuts in all possible channels by gluing simplified on-shell tree amplitudes together. This is especially simple when all particles are massless, although see for instance [131] on the massive case.

*Figure 30: The two cuts of the planar 4-pt SDYM amplitude.*

For a 4-pt massless planar color-ordered amplitude, the only non-zero cuts occur in the $s_{12}$ and $s_{23}$ channels. Let’s focus first on the $s_{12}$ , where we cut through the loop momenta $L$ and $L+p_{1}+p_{2}$ . We denote the 4-dimensional part of these $4-2\epsilon$ dimensional momenta as $\ell$ and $\ell+p_{1}+p_{2}$ . On this cut, we have the on-shell condition

$$ L^{2}=0,\hskip 14.22636pt(L+p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}=0. $$

This is equivalent to saying the 4-dimensional parts of the loop momenta have a mass $\mu^{2}$ :

$$ \ell^{2}=\mu^{2},\hskip 28.45274pt(\ell+p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}=\mu^{2}. $$

Now let us define the tree-amplitude $A^{\rm tree}(L,1^{+},2^{+},-L-p_{1}-p_{2})$ which satisfies the above on-shell condition. For simplicity, we imagine the $L$ and $-L-p_{1}-p_{2}$ legs to be “scalars” with no associated polarization factors. The two diagrams that contribute to this amplitude are drawn in figure 31.

*Figure 31: The two diagrams that contribute to $A^{\rm tree}(L,1^{+},2^{+},-L\!-\!p_{1}\!-\!p_{2})$*

Summing up the two diagrams, we get the following expression:

$$ \displaystyle A^{\rm tree}(L,1^{+},2^{+},-L\!-\!p_{1}\!-\!p_{1}) \displaystyle=\frac{i(\sqrt{2}g)^{2}}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle^{2}}\left(\frac{\langle{\alpha|\ell 1|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|(\ell+1)2|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{1})^{2}}+\frac{\langle{\alpha|12|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|\ell(1+2)|\alpha}\rangle}{\langle{12}\rangle[12]}\right). $$

This expression can be simplified using the following identity (proven in appendix F.3)

$$ \displaystyle\langle{\alpha|\ell 1|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|(\ell+1)2|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle=\frac{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle}{\langle{12}\rangle}\Big((\ell+p_{1})^{2}\langle{\alpha|\ell(1+2)|\alpha}\rangle-(\ell+p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}\langle{\alpha|\ell 1|\alpha}\rangle-\ell^{2}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+1)2|\alpha}\rangle\Big). $$

Using the cut condition (222) and the above identity, the tree amplitude simplifies to

$$ A^{\rm tree}(L,1^{+},2^{+},-L\!-\!p_{1}\!-\!p_{1})=i(\sqrt{2}g)^{2}\frac{\mu^{2}}{(L+p_{1})^{2}}\frac{[12]}{\langle{12}\rangle}. $$

Note that this amplitude is proportional to $\mu^{2}$ , which implies that it is zero in exactly 4-dimensions, as expected. Crucially, the above formula is also exact in general dimension $D$ , i.e. for all possible values of $\epsilon$ not necessarily small. The use of the exact tree amplitude in general $D$ is required in order for this method to produce the correct result.

For the 4-particle amplitude, the expression is simply a sum of the two cuts.

$$ \displaystyle A_{4;1}^{\text{1-loop}}(1^{+},2^{+},3^{+},4^{+}) \displaystyle=\int\frac{d^{D}L}{(2\pi)^{D}}\frac{i}{L^{2}}\frac{i}{(L+p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}}A^{\rm tree}(L,1^{+},2^{+},-L\!-\!p_{1}\!-\!p_{2})A^{\rm tree}(L\!-\!p_{3}\!-\!p_{4},3^{+},4^{+},-L) \displaystyle+\int\frac{d^{D}L}{(2\pi)^{D}}\frac{i}{L^{2}}\frac{i}{(L+p_{2}+p_{3})^{2}}A^{\rm tree}(L,2^{+},3^{+},-L\!-\!p_{2}\!-\!p_{3})A^{\rm tree}(L\!-\!p_{4}\!-\!p_{1},4^{+},1^{+},-L). $$

(A factor of 2 for the two polarizations of particles which can run across the cut is cancelled by an identical particle phase space factor of 1/2.)

For more than 4 particles, however, the amplitude is not simply a sum over cuts as shown above. This is, of course, because the tree-amplitudes themselves generically contain multi-particle propagators which will affect the values of other cuts. In general the difficulty comes in engineering expressions that agree on all cuts. Nowadays this is often done using computer software such as BlackHat [137].

In any case, for 4 particles the expression becomes

$$ \displaystyle A_{4;1}^{\text{1-loop}}(1^{+},2^{+},3^{+},4^{+}) \displaystyle=\frac{[12]}{\langle{12}\rangle}\frac{[34]}{\langle{34}\rangle}(\sqrt{2}g)^{4}\int\frac{d^{D}L}{(2\pi)^{D}}\frac{\mu^{4}}{L^{2}(L+p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}(L+p_{1})^{2}(L-p_{4})^{2}} \displaystyle+\frac{[23]}{\langle{23}\rangle}\frac{[41]}{\langle{41}\rangle}(\sqrt{2}g)^{4}\int\frac{d^{D}L}{(2\pi)^{D}}\frac{\mu^{4}}{L^{2}(L+p_{2}+p_{3})^{2}(L+p_{2})^{2}(L-p_{1})^{2}}. $$

The integrals are easy to evaluate and give

$$ A_{4;1}^{\text{1-loop}}(1^{+},2^{+},3^{+},4^{+})=\frac{-i(\sqrt{2}g)^{4}}{6(4\pi)^{2}}\left(\frac{[12]}{\langle{12}\rangle}\frac{[34]}{\langle{34}\rangle}+\frac{[23]}{\langle{23}\rangle}\frac{[41]}{\langle{41}\rangle}\right) $$

which is the correct expression.

## 13 One-loop-all-plus gravity expression of Bern, Dixon, Perelstein, Rozowsky

In this section we write down the nice closed-form expression for one-loop-all-plus SDG amplitudes, due to BDPR [50, 51], and explain where it comes from. We do not provide a proof of this formula because, at the time of writing this note, none exists. We expect the situation will be rectified in the near future.

Without further ado, the BDPR formula is

$$ \mathcal{M}^{\text{1-loop}}(1^{+},...,n^{+})=-\frac{i}{(4\pi)^{2}960}\left(-\frac{\kappa}{2}\right)^{n}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq a<b\leq n\\
A,B\end{subarray}}h(a,A,b)h(b,B,a)\tr^{3}[aAbB]. $$

We have checked numerically that the above expression matches equation (219) up to $n=9$ on the support of momentum conservation. In this formula, $A$ and $B$ are indistinguishable sets such that $A\cup B\cup\{a,b\}=\{1...n\}$ , $A\cap B=\emptyset$ , $a,b\notin A,B$ . We also have the definition

$$ \tr[aAbB]\equiv\langle a|p_{A}|b]\langle b|p_{B}|a]+\langle b|p_{A}|a]\langle a|p_{B}|b] $$

and define the “half-soft function” by

$$ h(a,\{1,2,...,n\},b)\equiv\frac{[12]}{\langle{12}\rangle}\frac{\langle a|p_{1,2}|3]\langle a|p_{1,3}|4]...\langle a|p_{1,n-1}|n]}{\langle{23}\rangle\langle{34}\rangle...\langle{n-1,n}\rangle\langle{a1}\rangle\langle{a2}\rangle\langle{a3}\rangle...\langle{an}\rangle\langle{1b}\rangle\langle{nb}\rangle}+\mathcal{P}(2,\!3,...,n) $$

where $p_{1,m}=\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_{i}$ and $\mathcal{P}(2,3,\ldots,n)$ represents a sum over all permutations of the denoted elements.

There are other nicer-looking presentations of the half-soft function [107]. These other presentations are equal to (231) identically, without the use of momentum conservation.77 7 To prove that the expression (231) is equal to these other expressions, all one has to do is show that all the expressions satisfy the same Berends-Giele recursion relation (236). Luckily for us, formula (231) was proven to satisfy it in appendix C.2 of [50].

If one defines the $n\times n$ matrix $\Psi$ via

$$ \Psi=\begin{cases}-\dfrac{[ij]}{\langle{ij}\rangle}\langle{ai}\rangle\langle{bi}\rangle\langle{aj}\rangle\langle{bj}\rangle&i\neq j\\
\displaystyle\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k=1\\
k\neq i\end{subarray}}^{n}\dfrac{[ik]}{\langle{ik}\rangle}\langle{ai}\rangle\langle{bi}\rangle\langle{ak}\rangle\langle{bk}\rangle&i=j\end{cases} $$

then the half soft function turns out to be equal to

$$ h(a,\{1,2,\ldots,n\},b)=\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\langle{ai}\rangle^{2}\langle{bi}\rangle^{2}}\right)|\Psi|^{i}_{i} $$

where $|\Psi|^{i}_{i}$ is the determinant of the minor of $\Psi$ where the row and column $i$ has been removed. The determinant is independent of $i$ . Note that none of the $i$ ’s are equal to $a$ or $b$ . This equation was given in [95].

Using the matrix tree theorem, the half-soft function can also be rewritten [107] as the tree sum

$$ h(a,\{1,2,\ldots,n\},b)=\left(\prod_{k=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\langle{ak}\rangle^{2}\langle{bk}\rangle^{2}}\right)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{trees with }\\
n\text{ nodes}\end{subarray}}\prod_{\text{edges }(ij)}\frac{[ij]}{\langle{ij}\rangle}\langle{ai}\rangle\langle{bi}\rangle\langle{aj}\rangle\langle{bj}\rangle. $$

The “trees” in the above formula are graphically the same trees that we saw for the all-plus current in figure 12. Having said that, the rules for the edges are different, as they depend on $|a\rangle$ and $|b\rangle$ instead of $|\alpha\rangle$ . However, if we set $|a\rangle=|b\rangle=|\alpha\rangle$ , then the half-soft function is in fact equal to the all-plus current via

$$ \mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1,2,\ldots,n)=\left(-\frac{\kappa}{2}\right)^{n-1}h(\alpha,\{1,2,\ldots,n\},\alpha). $$

As one might expect from the above relation, the half-soft function also satisfies a slightly more general form of the Berends-Giele recursion relation that $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}$ satisfies, namely [98]

$$ p_{N}^{2}h(a,N,b)=\sum_{A,B|A\cup B=N}\langle{a|p_{A}p_{B}|a}\rangle\langle{b|p_{A}p_{B}|b}\rangle h(a,A,b)h(a,B,b) $$

where here $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and $a,b\notin N$ . As a final relation, if we imagine that all of the momenta now sum to zero, the half-soft function is equal, up to a factor, to the NSVW formula for the tree-level gravity MHV amplitude [97]

$$ \mathcal{M}^{\rm tree}(1^{-},2^{-},3^{+},\ldots,n^{+})=i(-\kappa/2)^{n-2}\langle{12}\rangle^{6}h(1,\{3,\ldots,n\},2)\Big|_{p_{1}+\ldots+p_{n}=0}. $$

Why the all-plus currents and the MHV amplitudes are so closely related is actually not so clear, although it is reasonable enough given that both expressions have similar soft and collinear properties.
