## Appendix A Plebański’s first heavenly equation

In this note we have exclusive worked with SDG in lightcone gauge. In this gauge, self-dual metrics take the form

$$ ds^{2}=4(dud{\bar{u}}-dwd{\bar{w}})+2\kappa(\partial_{w}^{2}\phi)d{\bar{u}}^{2}+4\kappa(\partial_{u}\partial_{w}\phi)d{\bar{u}}d{\bar{w}}+2\kappa(\partial_{u}^{2}\phi)d{\bar{w}}^{2} $$

where $\phi$ satisfies “Plebański’s second heavenly equation”

$$ (\partial_{u}\partial_{{\bar{u}}}-\partial_{w}\partial_{{\bar{w}}})\phi-\frac{\kappa}{2}((\partial_{u}^{2}\phi)(\partial_{w}^{2}\phi)-(\partial_{u}\partial_{w}\phi)(\partial_{u}\partial_{w}\phi))=0. $$

However, there is another important way one can parameterize self-dual metrics. This has not played a role in this note but we shall mention it anyway. It turns out that there always exists a coordinate system $(y^{j},\bar{y}^{{\bar{\jmath}}})$ , with $j=1,2$ , ${\bar{\jmath}}=\bar{1},\bar{2}$ , in which any self-dual metric can be written as

$$ ds^{2}=-4\,\partial_{j}\partial_{{\bar{\jmath}}}\,\Omega\,dy^{j}d\bar{y}^{{\bar{\jmath}}} $$

where $\Omega$ is the Kähler scalar and satisfies “Plebański’s first heavenly equation”

$$ \det( \partial_{j} \partial_{\bj} \, \Omega)=(\partial_{1}\partial_{\bar{1}}\,\Omega)(\partial_{2}\partial_{\bar{2}}\,\Omega)-(\partial_{1}\partial_{\bar{2}}\,\Omega)(\partial_{2}\partial_{\bar{1}}\,\Omega)=1. $$

The coordinates $(y^{j},\bar{y}^{{\bar{\jmath}}})$ are related to the lightcone coordinates by

$$ u=-\frac{\partial\Omega}{\partial\bar{y}^{\bar{1}}},\hskip 14.22636ptw=\frac{\partial\Omega}{\partial\bar{y}^{\bar{2}}},\hskip 14.22636pt{\bar{u}}=\bar{y}^{\bar{1}},\hskip 14.22636pt{\bar{w}}=\bar{y}^{\bar{2}}. $$

We note that we reviewed the first and second heavenly equation in more detail in Appendix B of [61].

Note that the flat metric corresponds to the potential $\Omega=y^{1}\bar{y}^{\bar{1}}+y^{2}\bar{y}^{\bar{2}}$ . If we therefore write $\Omega$ as a perturbation on top of flat space,

$$ \Omega=y^{1}\bar{y}^{\bar{1}}+y^{2}\bar{y}^{\bar{2}}+\frac{\kappa}{2}\psi, $$

then (306) becomes

$$ (\partial_{1}\partial_{\bar{1}}+\partial_{2}\partial_{\bar{2}})\psi-\frac{\kappa}{2}((\partial_{\bar{1}}\partial_{2}\psi)(\partial_{1}\partial_{\bar{2}}\psi)+(\partial_{1}\partial_{\bar{1}}\psi)(\partial_{2}\partial_{\bar{2}}\psi))=0. $$

The above equation looks extremely similar to Plebański’s second heavenly equation (304), but it is actually Plebański’s first heavenly equation! This formulation of SDG is commonly used in discussions of the N=2 string.

## Appendix B Covariant formulation of SDYM and SDG

In this note we defined SDYM and SDG as truncations of the Yang-Mills and Einstein-Hilbert action in lightcone gauge. From this we found simple ghost-free cubic actions for SDYM and SDG, but the procedure broke manifest Lorentz covariance, which is equivalent to gauge-invariance/diffeomorphism-invariance of the amplitudes. In concrete terms, the gauge choice fixed a preferred spinor $|\alpha\rangle$ which appears in the interaction vertex and the polarization vectors. Of course, because the amplitudes in SDYM/SDG match those of the full theory, the final amplitudes ultimately do not depend on $|\alpha\rangle$ and thus SDYM/SDG must be covariant even if it is not manifest at the level of the lightcone actions.

The question we now ask is, is it possible to define SDYM and SDG as truncations of Yang-Mills theory/Einstein gravity in a manifestly covariant way? The answer is of course yes, and in this section we discuss the covariant formulations for SDYM and SDG.

As a consistency check, we will also show how, by gauge fixing the self-dual covariant actions, we can again rederive the same lightcone actions from before. So, truncating the theory first and then gauge fixing produces the same Lagrangian as gauge fixing first and then truncating.

### B.1 Covariant SDYM action

Recall that (flat) spacetime indices can be exchanged for spinor-helicity indices via

$$ V_{A\dot{A}}=\sigma_{A\dot{A}}^{\mu}V_{\mu},\hskip 28.45274ptV_{\mu}=\frac{1}{2}\sigma_{\mu}^{A\dot{A}}V_{A\dot{A}}. $$

It is a standard exercise to show that, in spinor variables, any antisymmetric tensor like $F_{\mu\nu}$ can be decomposed as

$$ F_{A\dot{A}B\dot{B}}=2\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}F_{AB}+2\varepsilon_{AB}\widetilde{F}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}} $$

where $F_{AB}=F_{(AB)}$ , $\widetilde{F}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=\widetilde{F}_{(\dot{A}\dot{B})}$ are symmetric tensors with 3 independent degrees of freedom each.

In fact, $F_{AB}$ represent the anti-self-dual degrees of freedom of $F_{\mu\nu}$ while $\widetilde{F}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}$ represent the self-dual degrees of freedom. This is easy to check if one uses the expression for the flat space $\varepsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$ pseudotensor in spinor indices,

$$ \varepsilon_{A\dot{A}B\dot{B}C\dot{C}D\dot{D}}=4i\,\varepsilon_{AC}\varepsilon_{BD}\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\varepsilon_{\dot{C}\dot{D}}-4i\,\varepsilon_{AB}\varepsilon_{CD}\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{C}}\varepsilon_{\dot{B}\dot{D}}. $$

Using $V^{\mu}W_{\mu}=\frac{1}{2}V^{A\dot{A}}W_{A\dot{A}}$ , we can compute

$$ \displaystyle F^{\mu\nu}F_{\mu\nu} \displaystyle=2F^{AB}F_{AB}+2\widetilde{F}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\widetilde{F}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\,, \displaystyle\varepsilon_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}F^{\mu\nu}F^{\rho\sigma} \displaystyle=4i\,(F^{AB}F_{AB}-\widetilde{F}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\widetilde{F}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}})\,. $$

The second term is the well known topological term $F\wedge F$ . We can add any multiple of it to the Yang-Mills action without affecting scattering amplitudes. Doing so, we can write the action of Yang-Mills theory, plus the topological term, in terms of only the anti-self-dual component $F_{AB}$ as

$$ S_{\rm YM}[A_{A\dot{A}}]=-\int d^{4}x\tr( F^{AB} F_{AB} ). $$

There is another way, however, to write this action. Introducing a new anti-self-dual field $B_{AB}$ , with $B_{AB}=B_{(AB)}$ , we write

$$ S_{\rm YM}[A_{A\dot{A}},B_{AB}]=-2\int d^{4}x\tr( B^{AB} F_{AB} - \frac{1}{2} B^{AB} B_{AB} ). $$

In this action, the independent fields are $B_{AB}$ and the usual gauge field $A_{A\dot{A}}$ , which enters the action via $F_{AB}$ from

$$ -4F_{AB}=\partial_{A\dot{A}}A_{B}^{\;\;\dot{A}}+\partial_{B\dot{A}}A_{A}^{\;\;\dot{A}}-ig[A_{A\dot{A}},A_{B}^{\;\;\dot{A}}]. $$

The equation of motion for $\delta B_{AB}$ from (315) is

$$ B_{AB}=F_{AB} $$

and plugging this back into the action, we recover (314). The above equation implies that on-shell, $B_{AB}$ should be thought of as a negative-helicity degree of freedom.

The covariant action for SDYM is defined by removing the $\tr B^{2}$ term in the YM action. It is

$$ \boxed{S_{\rm SDYM}[A_{A\dot{A}},B_{AB}]=-2\int d^{4}x\tr( B^{AB} F_{AB}).} $$

The $B_{AB}$ field is now takes the form of a Lagrange multiplier whose equation of motion enforces the self-duality equation $F_{AB}=0$ for the field $A_{A\dot{A}}$ .

If one varies $A_{A\dot{A}}$ in the SDYM action, one finds the equation of motion for $B_{AB}$ is

$$ 0=\partial_{A\dot{A}}B^{AB}-ig[A_{A\dot{A}},B^{AB}]=0. $$

This equation can also be written as $D_{A\dot{A}}B^{AB}=0$ where here $D_{A\dot{A}}$ is the covariant derivative of the self-dual field $A_{A\dot{A}}$ . If one substitutes in $F_{AB}$ for $B_{AB}$ in the above equation, one can show that this equation is a linear combination of the usual Yang-Mills e.o.m. $D_{\mu}F^{\mu\nu}=0$ and the Bianchi identity $\varepsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}D_{\mu}F_{\nu\rho}=0$ , on the self-dual background, that keeps only the anti-self-dual component of the field to the first linearized order. Our point is that the equation $B_{AB}=F_{AB}$ , which held for the full action but seemingly fails for the self-dual action when $A_{A\dot{A}}$ is self-dual and $F_{AB}=0$ , is still morally true. This is because $B_{AB}$ is behaving like a linearized anti-self-dual degree of freedom propagating on a self-dual background, and is evidently equal to the $F_{AB}$ of such a perturbation.

### B.2 SDYM gauge fixing

We now gauge fix the action (318) in lightcone gauge. The gauge fixing condition is

$$ \alpha^{A}\tilde{\alpha}^{\dot{A}}A_{A\dot{A}}=0. $$

We could introduce a Lagrange multiplier and $b$ $c$ ghost system to the action. However it is clear that the ghost system will decouple because the gauge variation of the above condition is $A$ -independent. See for instance our more explicit discussion in section 4.

Imposing the gauge fixing condition (320), we will now integrate out some components of $B_{AB}$ .

Let us define a new spinor $\beta^{A}$ such that

$$ \alpha^{A}\beta_{A}=1 $$

which implies the completeness relation

$$ \delta^{A}_{B}=-\alpha_{B}\beta^{A}+\beta_{B}\alpha^{A}. $$

In components,

$$ \alpha^{A}=(0,1),\hskip 14.22636pt\beta^{A}=(1,0),\hskip 14.22636pt\alpha_{A}=(-1,0),\hskip 14.22636pt\beta_{A}=(0,1), $$

and also $\tilde{\alpha}^{\dot{A}}=(0,1)$ . So the gauge condition (320) is

$$ A_{2\dot{2}}=0. $$

Let now decompose the $B_{AB}$ field into three independent degrees of freedom $(B,B^{\prime},B^{\prime\prime})$ as

$$ B_{AB}=B\alpha_{A}\alpha_{B}+B^{\prime}(\alpha_{A}\beta_{B}+\beta_{A}\alpha_{B})+B^{\prime\prime}\beta_{A}\beta_{B} $$

and let us now integrate out the component $B$ . The equation of motion for $\delta B=0$ is

$$ 0=-2F_{22}=\partial_{2\dot{A}}A_{2}^{\;\;\dot{A}}=-\partial_{2\dot{2}}A_{2\dot{1}} $$

which implies $A_{2\dot{1}}=0$ . Integrating $B$ out of the action, we therefore see that in the self-dual theory (324) is promoted to the two-component condition

$$ A_{2\dot{A}}=0 $$

which means we can write $A_{A\dot{A}}$ as

$$ A_{A\dot{A}}=\alpha_{A}A_{\dot{A}} $$

for some $A_{\dot{A}}$ .

Now we want to integrate out $B^{\prime}$ . Before we do this, however, let us introduce the symbols

$$ \displaystyle(\alpha\partial)_{\dot{A}} \displaystyle\equiv-\alpha^{A}\partial_{A\dot{A}}\,,\hskip 28.45274pt(\alpha\partial)^{\dot{A}}\,\equiv\alpha_{A}\partial^{A\dot{A}}\,, \displaystyle(\beta\partial)_{\dot{A}} \displaystyle=-\beta^{A}\partial_{A\dot{A}}\,,\hskip 28.45274pt(\beta\partial)^{\dot{A}}=\beta_{A}\partial^{A\dot{A}}\,. $$

(We include the relative sign so that $(\alpha\partial)_{\dot{A}}$ behaves as a proper spinor under raising and lowering, due to the sign in $\alpha^{A}\lambda_{A}=-\alpha_{A}\lambda^{A}$ .)

With these symbols, the decomposition of the identity (322) for instance implies

$$ \Box=\frac{1}{2}\partial_{A\dot{A}}\partial^{A\dot{A}}=(\beta\partial)_{\dot{A}}(\alpha\partial)^{\dot{A}}, $$

where lightcone coordinates, we recall

$$ \partial_{A\dot{A}}=\begin{pmatrix}\partial_{1\dot{1}}&\partial_{1\dot{2}}\\
\partial_{2\dot{1}}&\partial_{2\dot{2}}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\partial_{\bar{u}}&\partial_{\bar{w}}\\
\partial_{w}&\partial_{u}\end{pmatrix}. $$

The equation of motion for $\delta B^{\prime}$ is now

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=-2(\alpha^{A}\beta^{B}+\alpha^{B}\beta^{A})F_{AB} \displaystyle=(\alpha\partial)_{\dot{A}}A^{\dot{A}}. $$

Integrating out $B^{\prime}$ therefore implies that $A_{\dot{A}}$ can be expressed as

$$ A_{\dot{A}}=\sqrt{2}(\alpha\partial)_{\dot{A}}\Phi $$

for some potential $\Phi$ . Now we are just left with the last component $B^{\prime\prime}$ . For this component, let us substitute in

$$ B^{\prime\prime}=-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\bar{\Phi}. $$

We now compute that the gauge fixed action is

$$ \displaystyle S_{\rm SDYM}[\Phi,\bar{\Phi}] \displaystyle=-2\int d^{4}x\tr( B'' \beta^A \beta^B F_{AB} ) \displaystyle=-\int d^{4}x\tr\bar{\Phi}\left(\Box\,\Phi-\frac{ig}{\sqrt{2}}[(\alpha\partial)_{\dot{A}}\Phi,(\alpha\partial)^{\dot{A}}\Phi]\right) $$

and this is exactly the lightcone action.

### B.3 Covariant SDG action

In order to write down the covariant form of the self-dual gravity action, we first need to review the “chiral” formulation of full Einstein gravity due to Plebański [219]. See also the paper of Capovilla, Dell, Jacobsen, and Mason [220]. This construction possesses a number of subtleties which we discuss below.

This construction is expressed in terms of the tetrad 1-form, the anti-self-dual 2-forms, the spin-connection 1-form, and the Riemann curvature 2-form. We wrote a pedagogical introduction to these objects in appendix B of [61] and so we won’t review them too deeply again. Note that we use the same conventions from that appendix here. If we define the flat-space vierbein indices $a=0,1,2,3$ , which can be raised and lowered with the flat-space metric $\eta_{ab}$ , then we denote the tetrad 1-form as $\theta^{a}$ , spin-connection 1-form as $\Gamma_{ab}$ , and Riemann curvature 2-form $R_{ab}$ as, with

$$ \displaystyle\theta^{a} \displaystyle=\theta^{a}_{\mu}dx^{\mu}\,. \displaystyle\Gamma_{ab} \displaystyle=\Gamma_{ab\mu}dx^{\mu}\,. \displaystyle R_{ab} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}R_{ab\mu\nu}dx^{\mu}\wedge dx^{\nu}\,. $$

$\Gamma_{ab}=\Gamma_{[ab]}$ , $R_{ab}=R_{[ab]}$ are antisymmetric in the vierbein indices. $R_{ab}$ is a function of $\Gamma_{ab}$ , defined by

$$ R_{ab}\equiv\differential\Gamma_{ab}+\Gamma_{ac}\wedge\Gamma^{c}_{\;\;b}. $$

Note the metric is constructed out of the tetrads via $g_{\mu\nu}=\eta_{ab}\theta^{a}_{\mu}\theta^{b}_{\nu}$ . Note also $\theta^{a}_{\mu}\theta_{a}^{\nu}=\delta_{\mu}^{\nu}$ and $\theta^{a}_{\mu}\theta_{b}^{\mu}=\delta^{a}_{b}$ .

These objects can be used to construct the usual tetradic Palatini action for Einstein general relativity, which is

$$ S_{\rm GR\,(Palatini)}[\Gamma_{ab},\theta^{a}]=\frac{1}{\kappa^{2}}\int\varepsilon_{abcd}R^{ab}\wedge\theta^{c}\wedge\theta^{d}. $$

$\varepsilon_{abcd}$ is defined by $\varepsilon_{0123}=1$ . The equations of motion from varying $\Gamma_{ab}$ and $\theta^{a}$ are

$$ \displaystyle\varepsilon_{abcd}D\theta^{c}\wedge\theta^{d} \displaystyle=0\,, \displaystyle\varepsilon_{abcd}R^{ab}\wedge\theta^{c} \displaystyle=0\,, $$

where the “torsion” $D\theta^{a}$ is defined by

$$ D\theta^{a}\equiv\differential\theta^{a}+\Gamma^{a}_{\;\;b}\wedge\theta^{b}. $$

It can be shown that first equation of (339) implies the torsion-free condition $D\theta^{a}=0$ .1010 10 Here is why. The equation is equivalent to $T^{a}\wedge\theta^{b}-T^{b}\wedge\theta^{a}=0$ where $T^{a}=D\theta^{a}$ is a 2-form. Take the interior product with the vector field $\theta_{b}^{\rho}\partial_{\rho}$ . This results in the equation $-2T^{a}+4T^{a}-(\iota_{\theta_{b}}T^{b})\wedge\theta^{a}-T^{a}=0$ , or $T^{a}=(\iota_{\theta_{b}}T^{b})\wedge\theta^{a}$ , and plugging this back into the original equation we find $T^{a}=0$ . When the torsion-free condition is satisfied, one can show that the components of the spin connection can be expressed as functions of the tetrads. In particular, if we define $\Gamma^{a}_{\;\;bc}$ via

$$ \Gamma_{ab}=\Gamma^{a}_{\;\;bc}\theta^{c} $$

and denote the components of $\differential\theta^{a}=\frac{1}{2}C^{a}_{\;\;bc}\wedge\theta^{b}\wedge\theta^{c}$ using coefficients $C^{a}_{\;\;bc}=\partial_{[\mu}\theta_{\nu]}^{a}\theta^{\mu}_{b}\theta^{\nu}_{c}$ , then the torsion-free condition can be shown to imply

$$ \Gamma_{abc}=\frac{1}{2}(C_{abc}+C_{bca}-C_{cab}). $$

This can also be expressed as

$$ \Gamma^{a}_{\;\;bc}=\theta^{a}_{\;\mu}\theta_{c}^{\;\nu}(\partial_{\nu}\theta_{b}^{\;\mu}+\Gamma^{\mu}_{\nu\rho}\theta_{b}^{\;\rho}) $$

where $\Gamma^{\mu}_{\nu\rho}$ is the usual Christoffel symbol defined by the metric.

So we see that once the torsion-free condition is satisfied, then the spin-connection 1-form is equal to the usual metric-compatible expression. This then also implies that $R^{ab}=\frac{1}{2}\theta^{a}_{\mu}\theta^{b}_{\nu}R^{\mu\nu}_{\;\;\;\;\rho\sigma}dx^{\rho}dx^{\sigma}$ where $R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$ is the Riemann-tensor of the metric. The second equation of (339) can then be shown to be exactly the Einstein equation $R_{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}R=0$ .

There is also a more general form of the tetradic action. It turns out we can add any multiple of a term called the “Holst” term to it, resulting in the action

$$ S_{\rm GR\,(Palatini+Holst)}[\Gamma_{ab},\theta^{a}]=\frac{1}{\kappa^{2}}\int(\varepsilon_{abcd}R^{ab}\wedge\theta^{c}\wedge\theta^{d}+\frac{2}{\gamma}R_{ab}\wedge\theta^{a}\wedge\theta^{b}). $$

Here $\gamma$ is an arbitrary constant. The equations of motion have now become

$$ \displaystyle\varepsilon_{abcd}D\theta^{c}\wedge\theta^{d}+\frac{2}{\gamma}D\theta_{a}\wedge\theta_{b} \displaystyle=0\,, \displaystyle\varepsilon_{abcd}R^{ab}\wedge\theta^{c}+\frac{2}{\gamma}R_{cd}\wedge\theta^{c} \displaystyle=0\,. $$

For generic $\gamma$ , these equations of motion are actually equivalent to those from the pure Palatini action. To see this, simply act $\varepsilon^{ab}_{\;\;\;\;ef}-\frac{1}{\gamma}\delta^{a}_{e}\delta^{b}_{f}$ on the first equation. It turns out to be $-4(1+\frac{1}{\gamma^{2}})(D\theta^{a}\wedge\theta^{b}-D\theta^{b}\wedge\theta^{a})=0$ which again just gives the torsion-free condition. Once we have the torsion-free condition, $R_{cd}\wedge\theta^{c}$ vanishes due to the Bianchi identity of the Riemann tensor, so the second equation in (345) is once again just the Einstein equation. Note however that if $\gamma=\pm i$ the above reasoning does not hold and we need to perform a separate analysis, a fact we’ll return to momentarily.

Therefore, the “Holst” term is, morally speaking, somewhat like the gravitational analog to $\tr(F \wedge F)$ . Because the action is quadratic in $\Gamma_{ab}$ , the spin connection can be integrated out exactly, and so the classical equivalence of the actions with and without the Holst term implies the quantum equivalence as well.

Furthermore, with the volume 4-form defined as

$$ \mathrm{dvol}=\frac{1}{4!}\varepsilon_{abcd}\,\theta^{a}\wedge\theta^{b}\wedge\theta^{c}\wedge\theta^{d}\,, $$

because the torsion-free condition implies $R_{ab}$ is that given by the Riemann curvature of the metric, one can show that it also implies

$$ \varepsilon_{abcd}R^{ab}\wedge\theta^{c}\wedge\theta^{d}=2\,R\,\mathrm{dvol},\hskip 28.45274ptR_{ab}\wedge\theta^{a}\wedge\theta^{b}=-\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}\,\mathrm{dvol}, $$

so the Holst term vanishes when $\Gamma_{ab}$ is torsion-free using Bianchi, $\varepsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}=0$ .

Now let’s introduce the spinor-index versions of these objects. The tetrad 1-forms are denoted

$$ \theta^{A\dot{A}}=\theta^{A\dot{A}}_{\mu}dx^{\mu} $$

and we can use them to define the anti-self-dual and self-dual 2-forms

$$ \Sigma^{AB}\equiv\theta^{A\dot{A}}\wedge\theta^{B}_{\;\;\dot{B}},\hskip 14.22636pt\widetilde{\Sigma}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\equiv\theta^{A\dot{A}}\wedge\theta^{\;\;\dot{A}}_{B}. $$

The full torsion-free equation with spinor-indices is

$$ \differential\theta^{A\dot{A}}+\Gamma^{A}_{\;\;B}\wedge\theta^{B\dot{A}}+\widetilde{\Gamma}^{\dot{A}}_{\;\;\dot{B}}\wedge\theta^{A\dot{B}}=0\,. $$

We now split up the spin connection 1-form into anti-self-dual and self-dual parts

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma_{A\dot{A}B\dot{B}} \displaystyle=2\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\Gamma_{AB}+2\varepsilon_{AB}\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}} $$

as well as the curvature 2-form

$$ R_{A\dot{A}B\dot{B}}=2\varepsilon_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}R_{AB}+2\varepsilon_{AB}\widetilde{R}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}, $$

where we have

$$ \displaystyle R_{AB} \displaystyle=\differential\Gamma_{AB}+\Gamma_{A}^{\;\;C}\wedge\Gamma_{BC}\,, \displaystyle\widetilde{R}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}} \displaystyle=\differential\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}+\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\dot{C}}\wedge\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{B}\dot{C}}\,. $$

Note that $\Gamma_{AB}=\Gamma_{(AB)}$ , $\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=\widetilde{\Gamma}_{(\dot{A}\dot{B})}$ , $R_{AB}=R_{(AB)}$ , $\widetilde{R}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=\widetilde{R}_{(\dot{A}\dot{B})}$ are symmetric in the spinor indices.

Using the spinor indices, the usual Palatini Lagrangian is equal to

$$ \displaystyle\varepsilon_{abcd}R^{ab}\wedge\theta^{c}\wedge\theta^{d} \displaystyle=iR_{AB}\wedge\Sigma^{AB}-i\widetilde{R}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\wedge\widetilde{\Sigma}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\,, $$

and the Holst term is

$$ \displaystyle 2\,R_{ab}\wedge\theta^{a}\wedge\theta^{b} \displaystyle=R_{AB}\wedge\Sigma^{AB}+\widetilde{R}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\wedge\widetilde{\Sigma}^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\,. $$

So if we set $\gamma=-i$ for the Holst term, we get a new action for Einstein gravity, called the Plebański action, which only depends on the anti-self-dual component of the spin connection:

$$ \displaystyle S_{\text{GR (Plebański)}}[\theta^{A\dot{A}},\Gamma_{AB}] \displaystyle=\frac{2i}{\kappa^{2}}\int(\differential\Gamma_{AB}+\Gamma_{A}^{\;\;C}\wedge\Gamma_{BC})\wedge\theta^{A\dot{A}}\wedge\theta^{B}_{\;\;\dot{A}}\,. $$

Something very peculiar has occurred here. The original Palatini action depended on both $\Gamma_{AB}$ and $\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}$ , while the Plebański action only depends on $\Gamma_{AB}$ . Nonetheless, we claim it is an action full Einstein GR.

If $\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}$ is unfixed by the action, how can this be? For instance, the $\delta\Gamma_{AB}$ equation of motion is

$$ \differential\Sigma^{AB}+2\Gamma^{(A}_{\;\;\;\;C}\wedge\Sigma^{B)C}=0. $$

This is a torsion-free condition for $\Gamma_{AB}$ , but not $\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}$ , which seems completely unfixed.

The answer is that there is, of course, a reality condition. $\Gamma_{ab}$ has 6 real degrees of freedom which are repackaged in the 3 complex degrees of freedom of $\Gamma_{AB}$ . These degrees of freedom are then conjugates of $\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}$ , so if $\Gamma_{AB}$ is torsion-free then $\widetilde{\Gamma}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}$ must be torsion-free as well. (In the self-dual theory, however, we can no longer have the reality condition.)

One could also make the argument that, because (344) is an action for Einstein gravity for generic $\gamma$ , it would be strange if there were a discontinuity in the physical observables of the theory between the limit $\gamma\to-i$ and the strict equality $\gamma=-i$ , given that none of the amplitudes depend on $\gamma$ .

The SDG action is then the truncation of the Einstein gravity action where one removes the term quadratic in $\Gamma_{AB}$ . It is

$$ \displaystyle\boxed{S_{\rm SDG}[\theta^{A\dot{A}},\Gamma_{AB}]=\frac{2i}{\kappa^{2}}\int\differential\Gamma_{AB}\wedge\theta^{A\dot{A}}\wedge\theta^{B}_{\;\;\dot{A}}\,.} $$

As desired, this action is manifestly covariant under global Lorentz transformations of the spinor indices.

How do we see that this action describes self-dual gravity? Well, $\Gamma_{AB}$ plays the role of a Lagrange multiplier that enforces

$$ \differential\Sigma^{AB}=0\,. $$

If one then uses the torsion-free condition for the spin connection (357), this implies

$$ \Gamma_{AB}=0 $$

which then implies

$$ R_{AB}=0 $$

and this is the condition that the spacetime is self-dual.

However, we mention that the geometrically-defined $\Gamma_{AB}$ appearing in (360) is different from the $\Gamma_{AB}$ appearing in the self-dual action (358). This is because the torsion-free condition for $\Gamma_{AB}$ with repsect to $\theta^{A\dot{A}}$ (357) is not actually an equation of motion of the self-dual action (358). The situation is exactly analogous to what we encountered with the $B_{AB}$ field in the Yang-Mills action. After truncation to the self-dual action, this field no longer satisfied $B_{AB}=F_{AB}$ and instead acted as a Lagrange multiplier enforcing the self-duality of $A_{A\dot{A}}$ . Likewise for gravity, after the truncation, $\Gamma_{AB}$ no longer satisfies the torsion-free condition with respect to $\theta^{A\dot{A}}$ but now acts as a Lagrange multiplier enforcing self-duality on the spacetime defined by the tetrads $\theta^{A\dot{A}}$ . But afterwards, the variable $\Gamma_{AB}$ also acts as an anti-self-dual degree of freedom propagating linearly on this self-dual $\theta^{A\dot{A}}$ background.

We mention that there’s another way to see that the equation $\differential\Sigma^{AB}=0$ , in conjunction with the definition $\Sigma^{AB}=\theta^{A\dot{A}}\wedge\theta^{A}_{\;\;\dot{A}}$ , implies that the spacetime must be self-dual. If we define the components of the anti-self-dual-2-forms by $\Sigma^{AB}=\frac{1}{2}\Sigma^{AB}_{\mu\nu}dx^{\mu}\wedge dx^{\nu}$ , and define the (Lorentzian) almost-complex-structures $I$ , $J$ , $K$ , by

$$ I^{\mu}_{\;\;\nu}=\frac{1}{4}g^{\mu\rho}(\Sigma^{11}+\Sigma^{22})_{\rho\nu},\hskip 14.22636ptJ^{\mu}_{\;\;\nu}=\frac{i}{2}g^{\mu\rho}(\Sigma^{12})_{\rho\nu},\hskip 14.22636ptK^{\mu}_{\;\;\nu}=\frac{i}{4}g^{\mu\rho}(\Sigma^{11}-\Sigma^{22})_{\rho\nu}, $$

then from the tetrad definition of $\Sigma^{AB}$ we have the quaternionic relations $I^{2}=J^{2}=K^{2}=IJK=-1$ . Of course, these almost-complex-structures, which are just raised versions of the 2-forms $\Sigma^{AB}_{\mu\nu}$ , are actual complex-structures because the $\Sigma^{AB}$ are closed [221]. The 2-forms themselves are the associated symplectic forms and the manifold is Kähler. The quaternionic relations between $I$ , $J$ , $K$ , imply that the spacetime is actually Hyper-Kähler and therefore self-dual. We reviewed this in more detail appendix B of [61].

### B.4 SDG gauge fixing

Let us now explain how to gauge fix the SDG action (358) to lightcone gauge. I am not aware of a place where this exact computation has been worked out in the literature, and it is slightly subtle.

The Plebański action for GR (356) has two gauge symmetries: diffeomorphisms and local Lorentz transformations. Infinitesimally, the diffeomorphism symmetry is

$$ \displaystyle\delta_{\xi}\theta^{A\dot{A}}_{\mu} \displaystyle=-(\xi^{\nu}\partial_{\nu})\theta^{A\dot{A}}_{\mu}-(\partial_{\mu}\xi^{\nu})\theta^{A\dot{A}}_{\nu}\,, \displaystyle\delta_{\xi}\Gamma_{AB\mu} \displaystyle=-(\xi^{\nu}\partial_{\nu})\Gamma_{AB\mu}-(\partial_{\mu}\xi^{\nu})\Gamma_{AB\nu}\,. $$

Likewise, the infinitesimal local Lorentz symmetry is

$$ \displaystyle\delta_{\omega}\theta^{A\dot{A}} \displaystyle=\omega^{A}_{\;\;B}\theta^{B\dot{A}}+\widetilde{\omega}^{\dot{A}}_{\;\;\dot{B}}\theta^{A\dot{B}}\,, \displaystyle\delta_{\omega}\Gamma_{AB} \displaystyle=\omega_{A}^{\;\;C}\Gamma_{CB}+\omega_{B}^{\;\;C}\Gamma_{AC}+\differential\omega_{AB}\,, $$

where $\omega_{AB}=\omega_{(AB)}$ and $\widetilde{\omega}_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=\widetilde{\omega}_{(\dot{A}\dot{B})}$ are the anti-self-dual and self-dual components of the local Lorentz transformations.

The corresponding finite local Lorentz transformations act as

$$ \displaystyle\theta^{A\dot{A}} \displaystyle\mapsto\,\Lambda^{A}_{\;\;B}\theta^{B\dot{A}}+\widetilde{\Lambda}^{\dot{A}}_{\;\;\dot{B}}\theta^{A\dot{B}}\,, \displaystyle\Gamma_{AB} \displaystyle\mapsto\,\Lambda_{A}^{\;\;C}\Lambda_{B}^{\;\;D}\Gamma_{CD}+\Lambda_{\;\;A}^{C}\differential\Lambda_{CB}\,. $$

The matrices $\Lambda^{A}_{\;\;B}$ and $\widetilde{\Lambda}^{\dot{A}}_{\;\;\dot{B}}$ have determinant 1, which is equivalent to the inverse relation under raising and lowering $\Lambda^{A}_{\;\;B}\Lambda_{A}^{\;\;C}=\delta^{C}_{D}$ and $\widetilde{\Lambda}^{\dot{A}}_{\;\;\dot{B}}\widetilde{\Lambda}_{\dot{A}}^{\;\;\dot{C}}=\delta^{\dot{C}}_{\dot{D}}$ .

Note that the ASD spin-connection $\Gamma_{AB}$ does not transform “covariantly” under a local Lorentz transformation due to the inhomogeneous term. However, its curvature 2-form $R_{AB}\mapsto\Lambda_{A}^{\;\;C}\Lambda_{B}^{\;\;D}R_{CD}$ does transformation covariantly, which implies the invariance of the GR Plebański action.

An important point, however, is that the SDG action (358) is not invariant under the local Lorentz transformations where $\Lambda^{A}_{\;\;B}$ varies in spacetime. It does remain invariant under transformations where $\widetilde{\Lambda}^{\dot{A}}_{\;\;\dot{B}}$ varies, or under a global Lorentz transformation where $\Lambda^{A}_{\;\;B}$ is constant in spacetime. So we say that the SDG action has a $1\!/2$ -local-Lorentz gauge symmetry. This is because the action is not constructed out of the covariant object $R_{AB}$ , but only out of the non-covariant object $\differential\Gamma_{AB}$ . The non-covariance of the action can also be seen, for instance, in its equation of motion $\differential\Sigma^{AB}=0$ , which is not invariant under local Lorentz transformations with varying $\Lambda^{A}_{\;\;B}$ .1111 11 The SDG equation $\differential\Sigma^{AB}=0$ only holds in frames where the tetrads are chosen such that $\Gamma_{AB}=0$ . Such a frame can always be found on self-dual spacetimes, but for a more general frame one could have $\Gamma_{AB}=\Lambda_{\;\;A}^{C}\differential\Lambda_{CB}$ for some $\Lambda_{AB}$ .

Now we discuss how to fix the diffeomorphism+ $1\!/2$ -local-Lorentz gauge symmetry of the SDG action to lightcone gauge. This procedure is a bit subtle. Let us start by defining the “flat space” tetrads $\theta^{A\dot{A}}_{0}$ via

$$ \theta^{A\dot{A}}_{0}=\begin{pmatrix}\theta^{1\dot{1}}_{0}&\theta^{1\dot{2}}_{0}\\
\theta^{2\dot{1}}_{0}&\theta^{2\dot{2}}_{0}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}2d{\bar{u}}\,&2d{\bar{w}}\,\\
2dw\,&2du\,\end{pmatrix}. $$

The gauge condition we would probably like to set is $\alpha_{A}\tilde{\alpha}_{\dot{A}}\theta^{A\dot{A}}=\alpha_{A}\tilde{\alpha}_{\dot{A}}\theta^{A\dot{A}}_{0}$ . While this would be easy if we had the full diffeomorphism+local-Lorentz symmetry, it seems we cannot fix this gauge using the diffeomorphism+ $1\!/2$ local-Lorentz gauge symmetry we have. So we will take a different approach.

Let us introduce the gauge-fixing constraints

$$ G_{\mu\nu}\equiv\theta^{1\dot{1}}_{[\mu}\theta^{1\dot{2}}_{\nu]}-4\delta^{{\bar{u}}}_{[\mu}\delta^{{\bar{w}}}_{\nu]}\,,\hskip 28.45274ptG^{\dot{1}}_{\mu}\equiv\theta^{1\dot{1}}_{\mu}-2\delta^{{\bar{u}}}_{\mu}\,,\hskip 28.45274ptG^{\dot{2}}_{\mu}\equiv\theta^{1\dot{2}}_{\mu}-2\delta^{{\bar{w}}}_{\mu}\,, $$

where $G_{\mu\nu}=G_{[\mu\nu]}$ . The first constraint vanishes when $\theta^{1\dot{1}}\wedge\theta^{1\dot{2}}=4d{\bar{u}}\wedge d{\bar{w}}$ , and the last two constraints vanish when $\theta^{1\dot{1}}=2d{\bar{u}}$ , $\theta^{1\dot{2}}=2d{\bar{w}}$ . So any tetrads that make the latter two constraints vanish will also make the first constraint vanish, but we have a reason for breaking them up in this way.

Let us now introduce Lagrange multipliers $B^{\mu\nu}=B^{[\mu\nu]}$ and $B_{\dot{A}}^{\mu}$ in order to enforce these constraints. There will also be the usual $b$ $c$ fermions but we won’t write them out explicitly. The gauge fixed SDG action is

$$ \displaystyle S_{\rm SDG}^{\text{(gauge fixed)}}[\theta^{A\dot{A}},\Gamma_{AB},B^{\mu\nu},B_{\dot{A}}^{\mu},\text{fermions}] \displaystyle=\frac{2i}{\kappa^{2}}\int\left(\differential\Gamma_{AB}\wedge\theta^{A\dot{A}}\wedge\theta^{B}_{\;\;\dot{A}}+B^{\mu\nu}G_{\mu\nu}+B^{\mu}_{\dot{A}}G^{\dot{A}}_{\mu}\right)+S_{\text{fermions}}. $$

Note that it is straightforward to verify that the ghost fermions decouple from the rest of the action. This requires checking that the variations of our constraints under the diffeomorphims and $1\!/2$ -local Lorentz symmetries

$$ \delta_{\xi}G_{\mu\nu},\hskip 14.22636pt\delta_{\xi}G_{\mu}^{\dot{A}},\hskip 14.22636pt\delta_{\omega}G_{\mu\nu},\hskip 14.22636pt\delta_{\omega}G^{\dot{A}}_{\mu}\,, $$

decouple from the other fields on the support of the constraints, which is easy to do.

Now let us use the basis of spinors $\alpha_{A}$ , $\beta_{A}$ from (323) to decompose the spin-connection 1-form $\Gamma_{AB}$ into a triple of 1-forms we call $(\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime},\Gamma^{\prime\prime})$ via

$$ \Gamma_{AB}=\Gamma\alpha_{A}\alpha_{B}+\Gamma^{\prime}(\alpha_{A}\beta_{B}+\beta_{A}\alpha_{B})+\Gamma^{\prime\prime}\beta_{A}\beta_{B}. $$

Let’s start by integrating over the component $\Gamma\alpha_{A}\alpha_{B}$ . The variation of the action under $\delta\Gamma$ is

$$ 0=\frac{4i}{\kappa^{2}}\int\delta\Gamma\wedge\differential( \theta^{1 \dot 1} \wedge\theta^{1 \dot 2} ), $$

so $\Gamma$ is a Lagrange multiplier that sets $\mathrm{d}(\theta^{1\dot{1}}\wedge\theta^{1\dot{2}})=0$ . Now we integrate out the Lagrange multiplier $B^{\mu\nu}$ . This fixes the diffeomorphism gauge symmetry, setting $\theta^{1\dot{1}}\wedge\theta^{1\dot{2}}=4d{\bar{u}}\wedge d{\bar{w}}$ . Crucially, we know this can always be done via Darboux’s theorem, because $\theta^{1\dot{1}}\wedge\theta^{1\dot{2}}$ is a closed rank-two 2-form. In particular, the diffeomorphism degrees of feedom were used to set

$$ \theta^{1\dot{1}}_{u}=0,\hskip 14.22636pt\theta^{1\dot{1}}_{w}=0,\hskip 14.22636pt\theta^{1\dot{2}}_{u}=0,\hskip 14.22636pt\theta^{1\dot{2}}_{w}=0, $$

and we now have

$$ \displaystyle\theta^{1\dot{1}} \displaystyle=2(f_{11}\,d{\bar{u}}+f_{12}\,d{\bar{w}})\,, \displaystyle\theta^{1\dot{2}} \displaystyle=2(f_{21}\,d{\bar{u}}+f_{22}\,d{\bar{w}})\,, $$

for some functions $f_{11}$ , $f_{12}$ , $f_{21}$ , $f_{22}$ satisfying

$$ f_{11}f_{22}-f_{12}f_{21}=1. $$

(Not however that we still have the gauge freedom to modify the $u,w$ coordinates, which can be changed without affecting (373). This corresponds to the irrelevant choice of antiholomorphic reference spinor $|\tilde{\alpha}]$ .)

Now that we have integrated out $\Gamma$ and $B^{\mu\nu}$ and fixed our diffeomorphism symmetry, we turn to our $1\!/2$ -local Lorentz symmetry, which acts on the tetrads as $\theta^{A\dot{A}}\to\widetilde{\Lambda}^{\dot{A}}_{\;\;\dot{B}}\theta^{A\dot{B}}$ for $\widetilde{\Lambda}^{\dot{A}}_{\;\;\dot{B}}$ determinant 1.

Integrating out $B_{\mu}^{\dot{A}}$ completely fixes this remaining symmetry by setting $\widetilde{\Lambda}=(\begin{smallmatrix}f_{11}&f_{12}\\ f_{21}&f_{22}\end{smallmatrix})^{-1}$ . We are now left with

$$ \displaystyle\theta^{1\dot{1}} \displaystyle=2d{\bar{u}}\,, \displaystyle\theta^{1\dot{1}} \displaystyle=2d{\bar{w}}\,, $$

as desired. We have now gauge fixed the action. We can now express our tetrad as a perturbation on top of the flat space tetrads (366) via

$$ \theta^{A\dot{A}}=\theta_{0}^{A\dot{A}}+\kappa\,\alpha^{A}\chi^{\dot{A}} $$

for some 1-form $\chi^{\dot{A}}$ . Writing $\chi^{A\dot{A}}=\alpha^{A}\chi^{\dot{A}}$ , the SDG action is now

$$ S_{\rm SDG}[\chi^{\dot{A}},\Gamma^{\prime},\Gamma^{\prime\prime}]=\frac{2i}{\kappa^{2}}\int\differential( \Gamma' (\alpha_A \beta_B + \beta_A \alpha_B) + \Gamma'' \beta_A \beta_B)\wedge\left((\theta_{0}\!+\!\kappa\chi)^{A\dot{A}}\wedge(\theta_{0}\!+\!\kappa\chi)^{B}_{\;\;\dot{A}}\right). $$

Using the basis of spinors $\alpha_{A}$ and $\beta_{A}$ from (323), let us also define the 1-forms

$$ (\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{A}}\equiv\alpha_{A}\theta_{0}^{A\dot{A}},\hskip 28.45274pt(\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{A}}=\beta_{A}\theta_{0}^{A\dot{A}}. $$

Integrating out $\Gamma^{\prime}$ then implies

$$ \differential( (\alpha\theta_0)^{\dot A} \wedge\chi_{\dot A} )=0 $$

which, assuming a topologically trivial manifold and vanishing fall-offs for $\chi$ in the path integral, implies

$$ (\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{A}}\wedge\chi_{\dot{A}}=0. $$

Because $\{(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{A}},(\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{A}}\}_{\dot{A}=\dot{1},\dot{2}}$ are a complete basis of 1-forms, we can always express $\chi_{\dot{A}}$ as

$$ \kappa\,\chi_{\dot{A}}=X_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{B}}+Y_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}(\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{B}}\vphantom{\Bigg\rvert} $$

for some coefficients $X_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}$ , $Y_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}$ . The constraint (380) then implies that

$$ X_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=X_{(\dot{A}\dot{B})},\hskip 14.22636ptY_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=0. $$

Now that we have integrated out the $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma^{\prime}$ components, we are just left with $\Gamma^{\prime\prime}$ , and after an integration by parts the action is

$$ \displaystyle S_{\rm SDG}[\chi^{\dot{A}},\Gamma^{\prime\prime}]=-\frac{4i}{\kappa}\int\Gamma^{\prime\prime}\wedge((\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{A}}+\kappa\,\chi^{\dot{A}})\wedge\differential\chi_{\dot{A}}\,. $$

Let us now expand out $2\kappa\,((\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{A}}+\kappa\,\chi^{\dot{A}})\wedge\differential\chi_{\dot{A}}$ . To do this, we use the decomposition of the identity (322) to write the exterior derivative as

$$ \displaystyle\differential \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\theta_{0}^{C\dot{C}}\partial_{C\dot{C}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{C}}(\beta\partial)_{\dot{C}}-\frac{1}{2}(\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{C}}(\alpha\partial)_{\dot{C}} $$

and using this we compute

$$ \displaystyle 2\kappa\,\differential\chi_{\dot{A}} \displaystyle=\,-(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{B}}\wedge(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{C}}(\beta\partial)_{\dot{C}}X_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}+(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{B}}\wedge(\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{C}}(\alpha\partial)_{\dot{C}}X_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}. $$

Wedging this with $(\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{A}}+\kappa\,\chi^{\dot{A}}$ gives us

$$ \displaystyle 2\kappa((\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{A}}+\kappa\,\chi^{\dot{A}})\wedge\differential\chi_{\dot{A}}= \displaystyle-(\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{A}}\wedge(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{B}}\wedge(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{C}}(\beta\partial)_{\dot{C}}X_{\dot{A}\dot{B}} \displaystyle+(\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{A}}\wedge(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{B}}\wedge(\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{C}}(\alpha\partial)_{\dot{C}}X_{\dot{A}\dot{B}} \displaystyle-\mathchoice{{\displaystyle\mkern 0.0mu\vbox{\hrule height=0.5pt\vskip-8.80751pt\hbox{$\displaystyle(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{D}}\wedge(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{B}}\wedge(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{C}}\mkern-1.5mu$}}}}{{\textstyle\mkern 0.0mu\vbox{\hrule height=0.5pt\vskip-8.30751pt\hbox{$\textstyle(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{D}}\wedge(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{B}}\wedge(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{C}}\mkern-1.5mu$}}}}{{\scriptstyle\mkern 0.0mu\vbox{\hrule height=0.5pt\vskip-6.45676pt\hbox{$\scriptstyle(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{D}}\wedge(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{B}}\wedge(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{C}}\mkern-1.5mu$}}}}{{\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.0mu\vbox{\hrule height=0.5pt\vskip-5.40082pt\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{D}}\wedge(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{B}}\wedge(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{C}}\mkern-1.5mu$}}}}((\beta\partial)_{\dot{C}}X_{\dot{A}\dot{B}})X^{\dot{A}}_{\;\;\dot{D}} \displaystyle(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{D}}\wedge(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{B}}\wedge(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{C}}\mkern-1.5mu \displaystyle+(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{D}}\wedge(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{B}}\wedge(\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{C}}((\alpha\partial)_{\dot{C}}X_{\dot{A}\dot{B}})X^{\dot{A}}_{\;\;\dot{D}}. $$

Note that one of the terms is zero due to the relation

$$ (\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{A}}\wedge(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{B}}\wedge(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{C}}=0 $$

which follows simply because the dotted indices are two dimensional. Furthermore, we note the flat-space volume form is

$$ \mathrm{dvol}=\frac{i}{4}\theta_{0}^{1\dot{1}}\wedge\theta_{0}^{1\dot{2}}\wedge\theta_{0}^{2\dot{1}}\wedge\theta_{0}^{2\dot{2}} $$

and due to the index structure we also have

$$ (\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{A}}\wedge(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{B}}\wedge(\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{C}}\wedge(\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{D}}=-4i\,\varepsilon^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}\varepsilon^{\dot{C}\dot{D}}\mathrm{dvol}\vphantom{\Bigg\rvert}. $$

Using these relations, we can calculate

$$ \displaystyle(\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{E}}\wedge 2\kappa((\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{A}}+\kappa\,\chi^{\dot{A}})\wedge\differential\chi^{\dot{A}} \displaystyle=-4i\,((\beta\partial)_{\dot{C}}X^{\dot{C}\dot{E}}-((\alpha\partial)^{\dot{E}}X_{\dot{A}\dot{B}})X^{\dot{A}\dot{B}})\,\mathrm{dvol}\vphantom{\Bigg\rvert} \displaystyle(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{E}}\wedge 2\kappa((\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{A}}+\kappa\,\chi^{\dot{A}})\wedge\differential\chi^{\dot{A}} \displaystyle=-4i\,(\alpha\partial)_{\dot{C}}X^{\dot{C}\dot{E}}\,\mathrm{dvol}\,.\vphantom{\Bigg\rvert} $$

We now use the above two equations to rewrite (383). To do this, we expand out the spacetime coefficients of the 1-form $\Gamma^{\prime\prime}=\Gamma^{\prime\prime}_{E\dot{E}}\theta_{0}^{E\dot{E}}$ further into components via

$$ \Gamma^{\prime\prime}=(\alpha\Gamma^{\prime\prime})_{\dot{E}}(\beta\theta_{0})^{\dot{E}}-(\beta\Gamma^{\prime\prime})_{\dot{E}}(\alpha\theta_{0})^{\dot{E}}.\vphantom{\Bigg\rvert} $$

Plugging this in, we find

$$ \displaystyle S_{\rm SDG}[\Gamma^{\prime\prime},\chi^{\dot{A}}]=-\frac{8}{\kappa^{2}}\int \displaystyle\mathrm{dvol}\Big((\alpha\Gamma^{\prime\prime})_{\dot{E}}\Big[(\beta\partial)_{\dot{C}}X^{\dot{C}\dot{E}}-\frac{1}{2}(\alpha\partial)^{\dot{E}}(X_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}X^{\dot{A}\dot{B}})\Big] \displaystyle-(\beta\Gamma^{\prime\prime})_{\dot{E}}\Big[(\alpha\partial)_{\dot{C}}X^{\dot{C}\dot{E}}\Big]\Big)\,. $$

If we integrate out $(\beta\Gamma^{\prime\prime})_{\dot{E}}$ , this enforces

$$ (\alpha\partial)_{\dot{A}}X^{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=0.\vphantom{\Bigg\rvert} $$

In conjunction with the symmetry condition $X_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=X_{(\dot{A}\dot{B})}$ (382), this implies

$$ X_{\dot{A}\dot{B}}=\frac{\kappa}{2}(\alpha\partial)_{\dot{A}}(\alpha\partial)_{\dot{B}}\phi\vphantom{\Bigg\rvert} $$

for some potential $\phi$ . If we also define the $\bar{\phi}$ field as

$$ \bar{\phi}=-\frac{4}{\kappa}(\alpha\partial)^{\dot{E}}(\alpha\Gamma^{\prime\prime})_{\dot{E}}\,,\vphantom{\Bigg\rvert} $$

then with these substitutions, we now have

$$ \displaystyle S_{\rm SDG}[\phi,\bar{\phi}]=-\int \displaystyle\mathrm{dvol}\;\bar{\phi}\Big(\Box\,\phi-\frac{\kappa}{4}((\alpha\partial)_{\dot{A}}(\alpha\partial)_{\dot{B}}\phi)((\alpha\partial)^{\dot{A}}(\alpha\partial)^{\dot{B}}\phi))\Big)\vphantom{\Bigg\rvert} $$

which, as desired, is the lightcone action for SDG.

In terms of lightcone coordinates, if we unwrap the tetrads as a function of $\phi$ , we find they are

$$ \displaystyle\theta^{1\dot{1}} \displaystyle=2d{\bar{u}} \displaystyle\theta^{1\dot{2}} \displaystyle=2d{\bar{w}} \displaystyle\theta^{2\dot{1}} \displaystyle=2dw-\kappa(\partial_{u}\partial_{w}\phi)d{\bar{u}}-\kappa(\partial_{u}^{2}\phi)d{\bar{w}} \displaystyle\theta^{2\dot{2}} \displaystyle=2du+\kappa(\partial_{w}^{2}\phi)d{\bar{u}}+\kappa(\partial_{u}\partial_{w}\phi)d{\bar{w}}. $$

The tetrads can be used to calculate the self-dual metric via $g_{\mu\nu}=\frac{1}{2}\theta^{A\dot{A}}_{\mu}\theta_{A\dot{A}\nu}$ . Doing so reproduces (20).

### B.5 Another argument for the finiteness of the self-dual theories

In this subsection we sketch a slightly hand-wavy argument that the amplitudes of SDYM and SDG are finite, using the form of the covariant actions. Recall that the actions are

$$ \displaystyle S_{\rm SDYM}[A_{A\dot{A}},B_{AB}] \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\int d^{4}x\tr B^{AB}(\partial_{A\dot{A}}A_{B}^{\;\;\dot{A}}+\partial_{B\dot{A}}A_{A}^{\;\;\dot{A}}-ig[A_{A\dot{A}},A_{B}^{\;\;\dot{A}}])\, \displaystyle S_{\rm SDG}[\chi^{A\dot{A}},\Gamma_{AB}] \displaystyle=-\frac{4i}{\kappa}\int\Gamma_{AB}\wedge(\theta_{0}^{A\dot{A}}+\kappa\,\chi^{A\dot{A}})\wedge\differential\chi^{B}_{\;\;\dot{A}}\,, $$

where for the gravitational action we expanded the tetrad around flat-space via $\theta^{A\dot{A}}=\theta_{0}^{A\dot{A}}+\kappa\,\chi^{A\dot{A}}$ .

If we rescale the fields as

$$ \displaystyle B_{AB} \displaystyle\to g\,B_{AB} \displaystyle A_{A\dot{A}} \displaystyle\to g^{-1}A_{A\dot{A}} $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma_{AB} \displaystyle\mapsto\kappa^{2}\,\Gamma_{AB} \displaystyle\chi^{A\dot{A}} \displaystyle\mapsto\kappa^{-1}\chi^{A\dot{A}} $$

then the couplings $g$ and $\kappa$ drop out of the actions. As the physical observables of the theory can’t depend on any dimensionful factors, they ought to be finite.

Of course, at the quantum level, when we rescale fields in a path integral we should be concerned about generating an additional term in the action coming from anomalies in the measure. However, various consistency requirements imply that there are only a short list of terms that this anomaly can be. For SDYM, it turns out the anomaly is proportional to the topological term $\tr(F \wedge F)$ and for SDG it will also be proportional to a sum of topological terms. Because topological terms do not affect scattering amplitudes, the amplitudes remain unaffected by these anomalies. The topological terms do nonetheless run under the renormalization group, as discussed in for instance [179, 209, 222]. Other references on beta-functions and one-loop-determinants on non-trivial backgrounds are [4, 223].

## Appendix C Color factors of tree-level and one-loop amplitudes

In this appendix we will review how gauge theory color factors work at tree-level and one-loop-level, for the uninitiated. Say $N_{c}$ is the number of colors. We normalize our $\mathfrak{su}(N_{c})$ generators such that

$$ \tr( T^a T^b)=\delta^{ab}. $$

With this normalization, the matrices satisfy a completeness relation

$$ T^{a}_{ij}T^{a}_{k\ell}=\delta_{i\ell}\delta_{jk}-\frac{1}{N_{c}}\delta_{ij}\delta_{k\ell}. $$

See for instance [224] for a proof. The $\mathfrak{su}(N_{c})$ generators also satisfy

$$ \tr(T^a)=0. $$

We also, as always, have the cyclic property of the trace

$$ \tr(T^{a_1} T^{a_2} \ldots T^{a_n})=\tr(T^{a_2} \ldots T^{a_n} T^{a_1} ). $$

If our generators lived in $\mathfrak{u}(N_{c})$ instead of $\mathfrak{su}(N_{c})$ , then the identity matrix would be included in the list of generators and the completeness relation would be

$$ T^{a}_{ij}T^{a}_{k\ell}=\delta_{i\ell}\delta_{jk} $$

which is a simpler formula. (Note that the identity element does not satisfy (405).)

Even though our actual gauge algebra is $\mathfrak{su}(N_{c})$ , there is no harm in proceeding as if it is $\mathfrak{u}(N_{c})$ if we want to use the simpler completeness relation. This is because the $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ photon decouples from the rest of the particles in the Lagrangian. We will however only consider external gluons however which live in the original $\mathfrak{su}(N_{c})$ .

Now, with the structure constants

$$ [T^{a},T^{b}]=if^{abc}T^{c} $$

(403) implies

$$ \tr( [T^a, T^b] T^c )=if^{abc}. $$

From the cyclicity of the trace, one can show

$$ \tr( [T^a, T^b] T^c )=\tr( [ T^b , T^c ] T^a ) $$

which means that, whenever we have chosen our generators to satisfy (403), we also have the cyclic identity for the structure constants

$$ f^{abc}=f^{bca} $$

which means $f^{abc}$ are totally antisymmetric in $abc$ .

Let us now review the well-known story of color-ordering in tree-level and one-loop pure-gluon scattering amplitudes built out of cubic vertices. Our presentation will follow [225, 226]. See also [227].

A three-point gauge theory vertex is comprised of two parts: a structure constant $if^{abc}$ times a kinematic part. See, for instance our $(+$ $+$ $-)$ vertex in equation 104. Both parts are individually anti-symmetric in the three particles, and multiplied together they are completely symmetric. We will visually distinguish between these two factors by writing “color part” or “kinematic part” in the corner of all the diagrams. We will also draw the color diagrams with squiggly lines. See for instance figure 37.

*Figure 37: Splitting Feynman diagrams into a color and a kinematic part*

Let us now focus on the color part of the diagram. If we write $if^{abc}=\tr(T^a T^b T^c)-\tr(T^b T^a T^c)$ , we will split up each vertex into a difference of two vertices corresponding to the two color orderings, notated with an oriented circle. See figure 38.

*Figure 38: How to split up the structure constant into a sum of trace terms.*

We can then use the completeness relation (404) to reduce products of traces like $\tr( ... T^a)\tr(T^a...)$ where an internal color $T^{a}$ is being summed over into a single trace like $\tr(... \, ...)$ . We represent this diagrammatically in figure 39. This is the t’Hooft double line notation [228].

*Figure 39: Graphical representation of $\mathfrak{su}(N_{c})$ completeness relation (404).*

Of course, we can drop the $\propto\frac{1}{N_{c}}$ piece from figure 39 due to the $U(1)$ decoupling and only keep the double line. (If we wanted to keep the second piece, we would find that all of the terms associated with it would cancel pairwise anyway.) Note that the $\mathfrak{u}(N_{c})$ completeness relation (407) can be expressed as

$$ \tr( X T^a)\tr(T^a Y)=\tr(XY). $$

Now, consider a sum of color factor diagrams where some of the vertices are a clockwise “ $+$ ” circle and some of the vertices are a counterclockwise “ $-$ ” circle. There is, of course, a unique way to flip all of the counterclockwise circles into clockwise circles. By “flip”, we mean reverse the direction of the arrow and also switch the placement of one of the legs. See figure 40. This “flip” operation does not actually induce any sign, due to $\tr(T^a T^b T^c)=\tr(T^a T^b T^c)$ . See figure 41.

*Figure 40: Procedure for handling color ordering: flip all counterclockwise circles to be clockwise, which removes all signs and the positions of all external colors to similarly follow a clockwise pattern.*

*Figure 41: $\tr(T^a T^b T^c)=\tr(T^a T^b T^c)$ .*

After we “flip” all of the counterclockwise circles to be clockwise, the external particles will all have a well-defined cyclic color ordering. When we perform this same flip on the kinematic part of the diagram, we introduce a sign which happily cancels out the original sign of the counterclockwise circle.

This implies that when we sum over all Feynman diagrams, the expression will take the form of a sum over color orderings of the external particles, with an overall color factor $\tr(T^{a_1} \ldots T^{a_n})$ . We say that the full amplitude $\mathcal{A}$ can be written as a sum of “partial amplitudes” $A$ via

$$ \mathcal{A}^{\rm tree}(1,\ldots,n)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}/\mathbb{Z}_{n}}\tr(T^{\sigma(1)} \ldots T^{\sigma(n)} )A^{\rm tree}(\sigma(1),\ldots,\sigma(n)). $$

The rules to compute the partial amplitudes require one to fix the the positions of the external particles in a fixed clockwise color-ordering and remove the factors of $if^{abc}$ from the Feynman rules. Additionally, due to the antisymmetry of the kinematic vertices, if we mirror the diagram we have the reflection identity

$$ A^{\rm tree}(1,2,\ldots,n\!-\!1,n)=(-1)^{n}A^{\rm tree}(n,n\!-\!1,\ldots,2,1). $$

Now let us consider what happens at the one-loop level. Consider, for instance, figure 42.

*Figure 42: Color part of a 4-pt box.*

Here there are four external legs connected to a central loop. We now turn this diagram into a sum over $2^{4}=16$ diagrams with color ordered vertices. We then take the counterclockwise vertices and forcibly “flip” them, which makes the counterclockwise-outwards-pointing external particles now point inwards and be oriented clockwise. There will be two kinds of diagrams that arise from this process. The first kind will have all particles pointing completely outwards or completely inwards, such as in figure 43.

*Figure 43: One type of diagram that descends from figure 42, where the legs all point in or out.*

The second kind of diagram will have some of the legs pointing outward and some of the legs pointing inwards, such as in figure 44. (If only one leg is pointing inwards or outwards then the contribution will be zero because $\tr(T^a)=0$ .)

*Figure 44: Another type of diagram that descends from figure 42, where some legs point in and some legs point out.*

Taken together, one-loop amplitudes can be written as

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{A}^{\text{1-loop}}(1,\ldots,n)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}/\mathbb{Z}_{n}}N_{c}\tr(T^{\sigma(1)} \ldots T^{\sigma(n)} )A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n;1}(\sigma(1),\ldots,\sigma(n)) \displaystyle+\sum_{j=2}^{\lfloor\frac{n}{2}\rfloor+1}\sum_{\sigma\in S_{n}/\mathbb{Z}_{j-1}\times\mathbb{Z}_{n-j+1}}\tr(T^{\sigma(1) } \ldots T^{\sigma(j-1)})\tr(T^{\sigma(j)} \ldots T^{\sigma(n)})A^{\text{1-loop}}_{n;j}(\sigma(1)\ldots\sigma(n)). $$

All of the single-trace terms come from the diagrams where all legs are pointing outward or inward. (The inward diagrams just amount to color-order-reversed versions of the outward diagrams. In order to compare them directly, one can turn an inward-diagram into an outward-diagram by moving one of the edges of the loop through ‘infinity’ on the plane, which flips the circle inside-out without changing any orientations or incurring extra signs.) The double trace terms meanwhile come from diagrams where some legs point out and some point in.

The factor of $N_{c}$ in front of the single-trace terms comes from the fact that the inner or outer ring with no external particles contributes $\Tr(I)=N_{c}$ . This term dominates in the large $N_{c}$ limit.

The single-trace partial amplitudes $A_{n;1}$ are once again computed from planar, color ordered, Feynman diagrams where in the Feynman rules one drops the $if^{abc}$ vertex factors. The double-trace partial amplitudes $A_{n;j}$ for $j\geq 2$ are determined from $A_{n;1}$ by the formula

$$ A_{n;j}^{\text{1-loop}}(1,2,\ldots,j\!-\!1;j,\ldots,n)=(-1)^{j-1}\sum_{\sigma\in\text{COP}\{\alpha\}\{\beta\}}A_{n;1}^{\text{1-loop}}(\sigma(1),\ldots,\sigma(n)). $$

Here, $\alpha=\{j-1,\ldots,2,1\}$ and $\beta=\{j,\ldots,n\}$ . Note the ordering of the set $\alpha$ is backwards. The color ordered permutations $\text{COP}\{\alpha\}\{\beta\}$ is the set of all permutations that respects the cyclic color ordering of both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ , with $n$ held fixed in the last position. If $\alpha=\{3,2,1\}$ and $\beta=\{4,5\}$ , then all the permutations in $\text{COP}\{\alpha\}\{\beta\}$ are

$$ \begin{array}[]{cccc}(3,2,1,4,5),&(3,2,4,1,5),&(3,4,2,1,5),&(4,3,2,1,5),\\
(2,1,3,4,5),&(2,1,4,3,5),&(2,4,1,3,5),&(4,2,1,3,5),\\
(1,3,2,4,5),&(1,3,4,2,5),&(1,4,3,2,5),&(4,1,3,2,5).\end{array} $$

Let’s give the proof of (416). All one-loop diagrams look like trees coming off of a central loop, which we were instructed to flip to be inwards-pointing if the vertex circle at the base of the tree was counterclockwise.

It is clear by inspection that the form of (416) is basically correct, because all the diagrams that get added to the double-trace partial amplitudes have trees on an inside track (the $\alpha$ trees) and trees on an outside track (the $\beta$ trees). The factor of $(-1)^{j-1}$ comes from the signs involved in flipping the inside trees to the outside where they can be compared with the single-trace diagrams which are being summed over.

However there is one thing we have to check in order to prove (416). We have to check that if there are Feynman diagrams in $A_{n;1}$ where some of the elements of $\alpha$ and $\beta$ belong to the same tree, then they are “projected out,” summing to zero, by the sum over $\text{COP}\{\alpha\}\{\beta\}$ . This is because the only kinds of diagrams that contribute to the double-trace terms are diagrams where the trees with all- $\alpha$ legs point inwards and the trees with all- $\beta$ legs point outwards.

This is thankfully not hard to see. Consider a tree where some of the nodes belong to $\alpha$ and some to $\beta$ . Notice that the trees can all be paired up in such a way that they sum to zero, due to the antisymmetry of the kinematic Feynman rules. An example is drawn in figure 45.

*Figure 45: Partial amplitudes that have trees with leaves in both $\alpha$ and $\beta$ will cancel when summed over $\text{COP}\{\alpha\}\{\beta\}$ due to the antisymmetry of the stripped vertex. Here is one such cancelling pair.*

When we group the trees into pairs that cancel, those trees can be thought of as differing by elements of $\text{COP}\{\alpha\}\{\beta\}$ where one of the, say, elements of $\alpha$ has moved past a block of elements in $\beta$ at the highest level in the tree. The double-trace structure is invisible to such moves, but the color-stripped kinematic diagrams have a relative minus sign between the the two. Because any Feynman diagram with both $\alpha_{i}$ ’s and $\beta_{i}$ ’s sharing a tree is projected out by this sum, we have now proven (416).

We conclude the section by noting that the suggestive-looking double-lined diagrams with some external lines pointed inwards and some pointed outwards have an interpretation in string theory as vertex operators being placed on the inner-boundary or outer-boundary of an annulus-shaped worldsheet [229].

## Appendix D Derivation of Berends-Giele SDG current

In this appendix we show that the tree formula for the all-plus SDG Berends-Giele current (134), copied below

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(1,\ldots,n)=\left(-\frac{\kappa}{2}\right)^{n-1}\left(\prod_{a=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha a}\rangle^{4}}\right)\sum_{\text{trees}}\sum_{\text{edges }(ij)}\frac{[ij]}{\langle ij\rangle}\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha j}\rangle^{2} $$

solves the recursion relation (132), also copied below

$$ p_{N}^{2}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(N)=-\frac{\kappa}{2}\sum_{A,B|A\cup B=N}\langle\alpha|p_{A}p_{B}|\alpha\rangle^{2}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(A)\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(B). $$

We will show this by plugging (418) into both sides of the equation. We’ll use a proof from [61]. Another diagrammatic proof can be found in [93, 98].

On the RHS of (419), we have two factors of disjoint trees $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(A)$ and $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(B)$ we are summing over, where one of the trees has nodes in the set $A$ and the other tree has nodes in the set $B$ .

However, there is also a factor of $\langle{\alpha|p_{A}p_{B}|\alpha}\rangle^{2}$ in the sum. Let’s try to understand this factor graphically. Note that

$$ \langle{\alpha|p_{A}p_{B}|\alpha}\rangle=\sum_{a\in A}\sum_{b\in B}\langle{\alpha a}\rangle[ab]\langle{b\alpha}\rangle. $$

Pictorially, we can think of the factor $\langle{\alpha|p_{A}p_{B}|\alpha}\rangle^{2}$ as drawing two “squiggly” edges from one tree with nodes in $A$ to another tree with nodes in $B$ , where each squiggly edge from $a\in A$ to $b\in B$ corresponds to a factor of $\langle{\alpha a}\rangle[ab]\langle{b\alpha}\rangle$ . See figure 46.

*Figure 46: Definition of squiggly edge.*

A squiggly edge is the same as a normal edge, but multiplied by a factor of $\frac{\langle{ab}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha a}\rangle\langle{b\alpha}\rangle}$ . Note that the squiggly edge is oriented, as it is antisymmetric under the interchange $a\leftrightarrow b$ .

Our sum of disjoint trees can now be thought of as a sum of graphs with a single cycle in them, where there are two squiggly edges on the cycle. If $(kk^{\prime})$ and $(\ell\ell^{\prime})$ are two distinct squiggly edges in the cycle, then we write the RHS of (419) as

$$ \text{RHS}=\left(-\frac{\kappa}{2}\right)^{n-1}\left(\prod_{a=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha a}\rangle^{4}}\right)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{one loop}\\
\text{graphs}\end{subarray}}\left(\sum_{\text{edges }(i,j)}\frac{[ij]}{\langle{ij}\rangle}\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha j}\rangle^{2}\right)2\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(kk^{\prime})\in\text{cycle}\\
(\ell\ell^{\prime})\in\text{cycle}\\
(kk^{\prime})\neq(\ell\ell^{\prime})\end{subarray}}\frac{\langle{kk^{\prime}}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha k}\rangle\langle{\alpha k^{\prime}}\rangle}\frac{\langle{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha\ell}\rangle\langle{\alpha\ell^{\prime}}\rangle}. $$

The factor of 2 comes from the indistinguishability of the edges $(kk^{\prime})$ and $(\ell\ell^{\prime})$ . (Note that if we include $(kk^{\prime})$ , $(\ell\ell^{\prime})$ as a term in the sum, then we don’t also include $(\ell\ell^{\prime})$ , $(kk^{\prime})$ in the sum.) Note that both squiggly edges must point from the same component to the other, i.e. from an $A$ tree to a $B$ tree. We draw one such graph from “RHS” in figure 47.

*Figure 47: Pictorial representation of the RHS of (419).*

Let us now look at the LHS of (419) with the tree formula plugged in for $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(N)$ . Note that

$$ p_{N}^{2}=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\in N,b\in N\\
a\neq b\end{subarray}}[ab]\langle{ab}\rangle $$

so we can think of the quantity $p_{N}^{2}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(N)$ as a sum over tree graphs where we have added in one extra edge $(ab)$ which has its own special factor of $[ab]\langle{ab}\rangle$ . We will draw this as a double-lined edge, shown in figure 48.

*Figure 48: Definition of double-lined edge*

Note that the double-lined edge is a standard edge multiplied by $\frac{\langle{ab}\rangle^{2}}{\langle{\alpha a}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha b}\rangle^{2}}$ .

When we add the double-lined edge into the pre-existing tree graph from $\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(N)$ , the edge closes the tree into a one loop graph where $(ab)$ is an edge in the cycle. The LHS of (419) is then

$$ \text{LHS}=\left(-\frac{\kappa}{2}\right)^{n-1}\left(\prod_{a=1}^{n}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha a}\rangle^{4}}\right)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{one loop}\\
\text{graphs}\end{subarray}}\left(\sum_{\text{edges }(ij)}\frac{[ij]}{\langle{ij}\rangle}\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha j}\rangle^{2}\right)\sum_{(ab)\in\text{cycle}}\left(\frac{\langle{ab}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha a}\rangle\langle{\alpha b}\rangle}\right)^{2}. $$

We draw one such graph from “LHS” in figure 49.

*Figure 49: Pictorial representation of the LHS of (419).*

We can therefore show that the LHS equals the RHS if

$$ \sum_{(ab)\in\text{cycle}}\left(\frac{\langle{ab}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha a}\rangle\langle{\alpha b}\rangle}\right)^{2}\overset{?}{=}2\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}(kk^{\prime})\in\text{cycle}\\
(\ell\ell^{\prime})\in\text{cycle}\\
(kk^{\prime})\neq(\ell\ell^{\prime})\end{subarray}}\frac{\langle{kk^{\prime}}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha k}\rangle\langle{\alpha k^{\prime}}\rangle}\frac{\langle{\ell\ell^{\prime}}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha\ell}\rangle\langle{\alpha\ell^{\prime}}\rangle}. $$

However, from the Schouten identity (128), we know that

$$ \sum_{(ab)\in\text{cycle}}\frac{\langle{ab}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha a}\rangle\langle{\alpha b}\rangle}=0 $$

and squaring the above equation gives (424), completing the proof of (418). (Note that $(kk^{\prime})$ and $(\ell\ell^{\prime})$ both point from one connected component to the other. We need to reverse the direction of one arrow in order to make contact with the cyclic cancellation in (425). This introduces a minus sign necessary to make the equality (424) work.)

## Appendix E Derivation of collinear-limits recursion relation for SDG current

In this appendix we write down the proof of the collinear-limit based recursive formula for the all-plus gravity current, (151). Proofs can also be found in [98, 61, 38].

We write the formula again below.

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(|1\rangle,|1],\ldots,|n\rangle,|n]) \displaystyle=-\frac{\kappa}{2}\,\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}}{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle^{2}}\frac{[ni]}{\langle{ni}\rangle}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(|1\rangle,|1],\ldots,|i\rangle,|i]+\frac{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle}|n],\ldots,|n\!-\!1\rangle,|n\!-\!1]). $$

We will prove this using the tree-formula (418).

Let us think, diagrammatically, how to represent the RHS of (426). How can we represent a special node with angle bracket $|i\rangle$ and square bracket $|i]+\frac{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle}|n]$ ? Looking at the tree formula (418), we see that the square brackets only appear in the numerator. So, if some other node $j$ connects to this special node, then the square bracket term in the numerator $[ji]+\frac{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle}[jn]$ . This term can be thought of as the sum of two different trees, one where $j$ connects to a node $i$ and one where it more or less connects to a node $n$ .

However, because the whole term from this edge, accounting for the denominator, is $\frac{1}{\langle{ji}\rangle}([ji]+\frac{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle}[jn])$ , we see that the tree where $j$ connects to $n$ differs from a normal edge in two ways: (1) the denominator is $\langle{ji}\rangle$ instead of $\langle{jn}\rangle$ , and (2) there is also a factor of $\frac{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle}$ included.

Let us, therefore, define a new type of edge. We draw it in figure 50. It will have an arrow that points from $n$ to an adjacent node $i$ . We say the edge itself corresponds to a factor of $\frac{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}}{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle^{2}}\frac{[ni]}{\langle{ni}\rangle}$ , which comes from the prefactor in (426).

*Figure 50: Arrowed edge with special rule.*

The special rule for this edge is that, if some other node $j$ connects to $n$ , then that edge corresponds to a factor of $\frac{[nj]}{\langle{ij}\rangle}\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha j}\rangle^{2}\times\frac{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle}$ . This differs from a normal edge because $|n\rangle$ is replaced with $|i\rangle$ and we additionally multiply by a factor of $\frac{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle}$ . The arrow should be thought of as redirecting the angle bracket in the denominator from $|n\rangle$ to $|i\rangle$ . See figure 51.

*Figure 51: Rule for nodes which connect to $n$ , when $n$ has an arrowed edge.*

So, we can rewrite the RHS of (151) as a sum over trees with one arrowed edge that points from $n$ to some adjacent node $i$ . ( $i$ can be any adjacent node because we are summing over $i$ in (151).)

We will call all of these trees, with one arrow pointing from $n$ to an adjacent node, “arrowed trees.” An example is drawn in figure 52.

*Figure 52: An example of an “arrowed tree,” where an arrow points from $n$ to one neighbor.*

We can now write

$$ \displaystyle- \displaystyle\frac{\kappa}{2}\,\sum_{i=1}^{n-1}\frac{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}}{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle^{2}}\frac{[ni]}{\langle{ni}\rangle}\mathcal{J}_{\rm G}(|1\rangle,|1],\ldots,|i\rangle,|i]+\frac{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle}|n],\ldots,|n\!-\!1\rangle,|n\!-\!1]) \displaystyle=\left(-\frac{\kappa}{2}\right)^{n-1}\left(\prod_{a=1}^{n-1}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha a}\rangle^{4}}\right)\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\text{arrowed}\\
\text{trees}\end{subarray}}\sum_{\text{edges }(ij)}W_{(ij)} $$

where we define the “weights” $W_{(ij)}$ of the edges by

$$ \displaystyle W_{(ij)} \displaystyle=\dfrac{[ij]}{\langle{ij}\rangle}\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha j}\rangle^{2}\hskip 14.22636pt \displaystyle\text{if }i\neq n,j\neq n \displaystyle W_{(ni)} \displaystyle=\dfrac{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}}{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle^{2}}\dfrac{[ni]}{\langle{ni}\rangle} \displaystyle\text{if }(ni)\text{ is the arrowed edge }n\to i \displaystyle W_{(nj)} \displaystyle=\dfrac{[nj]}{\langle{ij}\rangle}\langle{\alpha i}\rangle^{2}\langle{\alpha j}\rangle^{2}\dfrac{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}{\langle{\alpha i}\rangle} \displaystyle\text{ if }n\to i\text{ is the arrowed edge and }j\neq i. $$

Now, when we sum over arrowed trees, we can also imagine ourselves taking a pre-existing tree, without an arrow, and then summing over all neighbors of $n$ , turning the edge from $n$ to that neighbor into an arrowed edge.

However, it turns out that we sum over all the placements of the arrow, it just equals the contribution of the tree without the arrow! This is depicted in 53. (Note that the RHS contains an extra factor of $\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle^{4}}$ necessary to make (427) match the desired expression.)

*Figure 53: The partial fractions formula implies that if we sum over all possible positions of the arrowed edge, the result is the same as the diagram with no arrow multiplied by $\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle^{4}}$ .*

Factoring out all the common prefactors, the validity of this sum boils down to the “partial fractions” identity

$$ \sum_{i=1}^{m}\left(\frac{\langle\alpha i\rangle}{\langle\alpha n\rangle}\right)^{m-1}\frac{1}{\langle ni\rangle}\prod_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=1\\
j\neq i\end{subarray}}^{m}\frac{1}{\langle ij\rangle}=\prod_{i=1}^{m}\frac{1}{\langle ni\rangle}. $$

This is a well-known identity, although we wrote down an inductive proof of it using the Schouten identity in Appendix A of [38].

## Appendix F Derivation of SDYM double-off-shell-current

### F.1 4-dimensional current

In this appendix we prove the closed-form expression (182) for the SDYM double-off-shell-current in exactly 4 dimensions. While we struggled to locate where exactly Mahlon wrote down the original proof, we did manage to come up with one nonetheless.

We copy the final result below as

$$ J_{\rm YM}(\ell\,;\,1,\ldots,n)=(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n}\frac{-i}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n-1,n}\rangle\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k})k|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}}\right). $$

Here $p_{i,j}\equiv p_{i}+p_{i+1}+\ldots+p_{j-1}+p_{j}$ and $p_{i,i-1}=0$ . Specifically, we will show that the above solution for the double-off-shell current satisfies the Berends-Giele recursion relation

$$ (\ell+p_{N})^{2}J_{\rm YM}(\ell\,;\,N)=i\sqrt{2}g\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=0\\
A=\{1,\ldots,j\}\\
B=\{j+1,\ldots,n\}\end{subarray}}^{n-1}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{A})p_{B}|\alpha}\rangle J_{\rm YM}(\ell\,;\,A)J_{\rm YM}(B) $$

where $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ and of course the single-off-shell-current is

$$ J_{\rm YM}(N)=(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n-1}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle}\frac{1}{\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n-1,n}\rangle}\frac{1}{\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}. $$

The base case $(j=0)$ for the double-off-shell current is

$$ J_{\rm YM}(\ell)=\frac{i}{\ell^{2}}. $$

Let us plug the above expressions into (431) and remove an overall factor of $\frac{(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n}(-i)}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n-1,n}\rangle\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}$ . On the left hand side, we get

$$ (**)=(\ell+p_{1,n})^{2}\left(\sum_{k=1}^{n}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k})k|\alpha}\rangle}{(\ell+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(\ell+p_{1,k})^{2}}\right). $$

On the right hand side, we have

We shall now manipulate $(*)$ and show that it is equal to $(**)$ . We use the color blue to highlight what changes from line to line.

### F.2 $4-2\epsilon$ -dimensional current

In this section we compute the $4-2\epsilon$ dimensional SDYM double-off-shell current $J_{\rm YM}(L;N)$ (188). This current is defined in by going up “one step” in the recursion relation for the double-off-shell current and replacing all the 4-dimensional propagators with the $4-2\epsilon$ -dimensional ones. We write

$$ J_{\rm YM}(L\,;\,N)\equiv\frac{i\sqrt{2}g}{(L+p_{N})^{2}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j=0\\
A=\{1,\ldots,j\}\\
B=\{j+1,\ldots,n\}\end{subarray}}^{n-1}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{A})p_{B}|\alpha}\rangle J_{\rm YM}(\ell\,;\,A)\Big\rvert_{\ell\,\mapsto L}J_{\rm YM}(B). $$

Note that the substitution $\ell\mapsto L$ does not affect the numerators of $J_{\rm YM}(\ell;A)$ , only the propagators in the denominator via the relation $(L+p)^{2}=(\ell+p)^{2}-\mu^{2}$ . Our goal then is to separate out all the extra terms generated by the identity

$$ \frac{(\ell+p)^{2}}{(L+p)^{2}}=1+\frac{\mu^{2}}{(L+p)^{2}}. $$

Anticipating this moment, we have conveniently isolated the only steps in the previous subsection where such a division occurs. The first place occurs at equation (447). The second place occurs at the end, after our penultimate equation (449), when we are to divide by $(L+p_{N})^{2}$ which cancels out an overall factor of $(\ell+p_{N})^{2}$ . Note also that we, in the final step of our proof in the last section, also multiplied a term by a factor of $1=\frac{(\ell+p_{1,n})^{2}}{(\ell+p_{1,n})^{2}}$ , which we must now replace with $1=\frac{(L+p_{1,n})^{2}}{(L+p_{1,n})^{2}}$ .

Let us bring all these terms together. We port the terms over from (449) in blue and write the additional terms generated by the cancellations of (447) in purple. The result is

$$ \displaystyle J_{\rm YM}(L\;;N) \displaystyle=\frac{(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n}(-i)}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n-1,n}\rangle\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}\Bigg( \displaystyle\color[rgb]{0,0,1}{\displaystyle\frac{1}{(L+p_{1,n})^{2}}\times\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,n-1})n|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{1,n-1})^{2}}+\frac{(\ell+p_{1,n})^{2}}{(L+p_{1,n})^{2}}\sum_{1\leq k<n}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k-1})k|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(L+p_{1,k})^{2}}} \displaystyle\color[rgb]{0.75,0,0.25}{\displaystyle+\frac{\mu^{2}}{(L+p_{1,n})^{2}}\sum_{1\leq k<n}\left(-\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k-1})p_{k,n}|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(L+p_{1,k})^{2}}+\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k})p_{k+1,n}|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(L+p_{1,k})^{2}}\right)}\Bigg). $$

Using the elementary simplification

$$ \displaystyle\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k-1})k|\alpha}\rangle-\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k-1})p_{k,n}|\alpha}\rangle+\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k})p_{k+1,n}|\alpha}\rangle=-\langle{\alpha|p_{k,n}k|\alpha}\rangle $$

the expression is equal to

$$ \displaystyle J_{\rm YM}(L\;;N) \displaystyle=\frac{(-i\sqrt{2}g)^{n}(-i)}{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{12}\rangle\ldots\langle{n-1,n}\rangle\langle{\alpha n}\rangle}\Bigg(\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\frac{\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1,k-1})k|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(L+p_{1,k})^{2}} \displaystyle-\frac{\mu^{2}}{(L+p_{1,n})^{2}}\sum_{1\leq k\leq n}\frac{\langle{\alpha|p_{k,n}k|\alpha}\rangle}{(L+p_{1,k-1})^{2}(L+p_{1,k})^{2}}\Bigg) $$

which is what we wanted to show.

### F.3 A useful Clifford algebra identity

In this appendix we are going to prove a very useful identity. First, it will be useful for us to define a certain spinor object constructed out of four momenta. The object is defined as

$$ \langle{\alpha|p_{1}p_{2}p_{3}p_{4}|\alpha}\rangle\equiv-\,\alpha_{A}\,(p_{1}^{\mu}\,\sigma_{\mu}^{A\dot{A}})(p_{2,\nu}\,\sigma^{\nu}_{B\dot{A}})(p_{3}^{\rho}\,\sigma_{\rho}^{B\dot{B}})(p_{4,\gamma}\,\sigma^{\gamma}_{C\dot{B}})\,\alpha^{C}. $$

Note the minus sign out front. Recalling that $\langle{ij}\rangle=\lambda_{i}^{A}\lambda_{jA}$ , $[ij]=\tilde{\lambda}_{i}^{\dot{A}}\tilde{\lambda}_{j,\dot{A}}$ , the minus sign is there so that, if all the momenta are on-shell, we get the natural equation

$$ \displaystyle\langle{\alpha|p_{1}p_{2}p_{3}p_{4}|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle\equiv-\alpha_{A}\,(p_{1}^{\mu}\,\sigma_{\mu}^{A\dot{A}})(p_{2,\nu}\,\sigma^{\nu}_{B\dot{A}})(p_{3}^{\rho}\,\sigma_{\rho}^{B\dot{B}})(p_{4,\gamma}\,\sigma^{\gamma}_{C\dot{B}})\,\alpha^{C} \displaystyle=-\underbrace{(\alpha_{A}\lambda_{1}^{A})}_{-1}(\tilde{\lambda}_{1}^{\dot{A}}\tilde{\lambda}_{2\dot{A}})\underbrace{(\lambda_{2B}\lambda_{3}^{B})}_{-1}(\tilde{\lambda}_{3}^{\dot{B}}\tilde{\lambda}_{4\dot{B}})\underbrace{(\lambda_{4C}\alpha^{C})}_{-1} \displaystyle=\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle[12]\langle{23}\rangle[34]\langle{4\alpha}\rangle. $$

This sign is not present in the two-momentum object because

$$ \displaystyle\langle{\alpha|p_{1}p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle=\alpha_{A}\,(p_{1}^{\mu}\,\sigma_{\mu}^{A\dot{A}})(p_{2,\nu}\,\sigma^{\nu}_{B\dot{A}})\,\alpha^{B} \displaystyle=\underbrace{(\alpha_{A}\lambda_{1}^{A})}_{-1}(\tilde{\lambda}_{1}^{\dot{A}}\tilde{\lambda}_{2\dot{A}})\underbrace{(\lambda_{2B}\alpha^{B})}_{-1} \displaystyle=\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle[12]\langle{2\alpha}\rangle. $$

Using the Clifford algebra relation $\{\sigma^{\mu},\sigma^{\nu}\}=2\eta^{\mu\nu}$ , and accounting for the relative sign in between the four-momentum and two-momentum object, for any momenta $P_{1}$ , $P_{2}$ , $P_{3}$ we have

$$ \displaystyle\langle{\alpha|P_{3}P_{1}P_{2}P_{3}|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle=-P_{3}^{2}\langle{\alpha|P_{1}P_{2}|\alpha}\rangle+(2P_{3}\cdot P_{2})\langle{\alpha|P_{1}P_{3}|\alpha}\rangle-(2P_{3}\cdot P_{1})\langle{\alpha|P_{2}P_{3}|\alpha}\rangle. $$

Now say $p_{1}^{2}=p_{2}^{2}=0$ and $\ell^{2}\neq 0$ . We are interested in expanding the quantity $\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1}|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1})p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle$ , which is a product of two-momentum objects, as a sum of such objects. We first massage the expression as

$$ \displaystyle\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1}|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1})p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle=\frac{\langle{1\alpha}\rangle\langle{2\alpha}\rangle}{\langle{12}\rangle}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1})p_{1}p_{2}(\ell+p_{1})|\alpha}\rangle $$

Now we plug in to (459) to get the following equation.

$$ \displaystyle=\frac{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle}{\langle{12}\rangle}\left(-(\ell+p_{1})^{2}\langle{\alpha|p_{1}p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle-2(\ell+p_{1})\cdot p_{2}\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1}|\alpha}\rangle+2\ell\cdot p_{1}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1})p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle\right) \displaystyle=\frac{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle}{\langle{12}\rangle}\left(-(\ell\!+\!p_{1})^{2}\langle{\alpha|p_{1}p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle-((\ell\!+\!p_{1}\!+\!p_{2})^{2}-(\ell\!+\!p_{1})^{2})\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1}|\alpha}\rangle+((\ell\!+\!p_{1})^{2}-\ell^{2})\langle{\alpha|(\ell\!+\!p_{1})p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle\right) \displaystyle=\frac{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle}{\langle{12}\rangle}\big(\!\!-\!(\ell\!+\!p_{1})^{2}\big(\langle{\alpha|p_{1}p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle\!-\!\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1}|\alpha}\rangle\!-\!\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1})p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle\big)\!-\!(\ell\!+\!p_{1}\!+\!p_{2})^{2}\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1}|\alpha}\rangle\!-\!\ell^{2}\langle{\alpha|(\ell\!+\!p_{1})p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle\big) $$

After one last simplification, we have now derived the very handy identity

$$ \displaystyle\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1}|\alpha}\rangle\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1})p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle \displaystyle=\frac{\langle{\alpha 1}\rangle\langle{\alpha 2}\rangle}{\langle{12}\rangle}\Big((\ell+p_{1})^{2}\langle{\alpha|\ell(p_{1}+p_{2})|\alpha}\rangle-(\ell+p_{1}+p_{2})^{2}\langle{\alpha|\ell p_{1}|\alpha}\rangle-\ell^{2}\langle{\alpha|(\ell+p_{1})p_{2}|\alpha}\rangle\Big).\;\;\;\vphantom{\Bigg\rvert} $$
